speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of importance under the terms of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the government underwrites, through CAHA, the development of junior hockey in Canada, and because foreign professional hockey teams have taken to raiding the junior ranks without in any way compensating for development fees which directly affect Canadian taxpayers, as witness last week, for example, in the signing of 17-year old Wayne Gretzky by the Indianapolis Racers of the WHA, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski):
That the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport introduce forthwith a program which would make it compulsory for all professional hockey teams and leagues drafting Canadian players to reimburse junior hockey in Canada to an amount equivalent to their over-all development and administrative costs.

speechtext:

Considering that under Standing Order 2(3), June 24 and July 1 are legal holidays on which there is no sitting of the House; considering that this year, June 24 and July 1 fall on a Saturday when usually parliament does not sit, and to prevent the staff of the House of Commons as well as members of parliament from losing the holidays on June 24 and July 1, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the International Whaling Conference commences in London on June 26 of this year, in view of Canada's failure in the past to support a moratorium in spite of worldwide scientific support for such a moratorium, in view of the decimation of the North Pacific sperm whale by Russian and Japanese fisheries, and in view of Canada's role in allowing a massive increase in North Pacific sperm whale quotas, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That the Canadian delegation to the London conference be instructed to end its support for whaling and to support a ten-year moratorium so that this magnificent creature can have some chance of survival.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF NEW LEGISLATION ON THE MONARCHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. However, he is not here and I direct it to the Deputy Prime Minister. Approximately three years ago, the Prime Minister made the statement in a speech in Quebec city that this government intended to achieve the end of the monarchy by placing the Governor General of Canada in the position of being able to do all those things that Her Majesty the Queen could do.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister, why did the government, having this idea in mind all that time, wait three years before doing the proper, appropriate and constitutional thing of advising Her Majesty as to the changes to be made? I also ask why the government has decided to place before parliament such a bill, when section 91 of the BN A Act reads:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Canada-
The proposed bill would delete the name and expression "The Queen" and substitute the Governor General of Canada in her place, thereby placing an end, in effect, to the monarchy in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege of which I have given you notice. It has to do with the case of Dr. Alexander Peter Treu.
In the first place I want to make my own position clear. I am acting as one of the legal counsel to Dr. Treu. I am receiving no fee now, nor will I be receiving any fee, so I have no pecuniary interest at all. 1 think the House is entitled to know this.

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-THE ALEXANDER PETER TREU CASE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-THE ALEXANDER PETER TREU CASE
speechtext:
I was greatly disturbed to read in Hansard some of the statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) yesterday in answer to questions asked by my hon. friend from Halifax and other members of this party. Either the right hon. gentleman was devious, or he was ignorant. Because of the rules of the House I will accept the latter explanation. As reported at page 6517, the Prime Minister said, in connection with the contracts Dr. Treu received after his persecution by the government had commenced:
The simple answer, as the Minister of Justice indicated, is that the contracts received from NATO during the latter period were not classified as confidential.
This is a very natural thing. These are commercial contracts and no one suggests that commercial contracts are classified. But out of those contracts received by Dr. Treu, while he was being prosecuted, while his documents were taken away during the two years of his trial, some 2,000 products and/or documents of a classified nature were processed by Dr. Treu and forwarded by him to the NATO centres at which they were received. The contracts may not have been classified but the end products were, to the extent of some 2,000.
In the second place, as far as I am able to gather in a limited time, Dr. Treu did receive at least two classified documents, one in April, 1975, and a second document dated June 21, 1976, after his trial had commenced, which he received with an attached list of a classified nature on June 26, 1976, and of course he sent the classified material back. So much for the question of classified documents.
Dealing with a further aspect, the right hon. gentleman said with regard to the security classification:
June 20, 1978

When he left the company his security clearance ceased by the very fact of his leaving.
Later on, as reported on the right hand side of the same page and speaking about Dr. Treu, the Prime Minister said:
" . .. he concluded he no longer had the clearance of that job ..
The facts are that in December of 1972 Northern Electric, with whom Dr. Treu had been working as one of the advisers in connection with a most complex and useful scheme in relation to the NATO countries, of which Canada is still a part, got out of the business. At the strong urging of both the government and Northern Electric a company was formed by Dr. Treu to take over in December of 1972.
In June of 1973 Dr. Treu was among those attending a security meeting of a classified nature where he was "badged" and security cleared, and during which he talked to Mr. Jenkyns, the security clearance officer acting as liaison with NATO. Mr. Jenkyns was the security officer for the Department of Supply and Services. In June of 1974, Dr. Treu, security cleared and wearing his badge, attended a similar meeting. Finally, a letter dated January 5, 1976, over the signature of Hugh Grant, director of the defence programs branch of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, invited Dr. Treu to attend a meeting of that branch which was to be held in Ottawa during the week of April 5, 1976.
I sincerely hope that the Prime Minister will set the record straight with respect to these issues, and I hope that, as he continues to play around with his constitutional tinkertoys, someone who has some knowledge of the law and human rights and natural justice will see that the proper kind of arrangements are written into the constitution in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman stated at the beginning of his question of privilege that he was acting on behalf of a person who is pleading his case before the appeal court. Obviously he is acting as a lawyer properly should before the courts. He is pleading the case of his client. The courts have already decided the client is guilty under the law. I take it that if the lawyer opposite us wants to continue pleading the case, he can go before the courts and do so.
The hon. member is now presenting a case not as a member of parliament but as a party to litigation in a criminal matter. He is apparently giving evidence which he got from his client. I have contrary evidence. I have evidence from the government that the contracts received from NATO during that period were not in classified areas. In some subtle way the hon. member admits this, but he says the results of the contracts, presumably work that Mr. Treu did, ended up being classified, I suppose by NATO. That is not surprising. A person who is not classified can do work for a government or for the private sector, or for an international organization, which can then decide to classify it. The person doing the work is not the one who is going to decide whether the receiver of the work will communicate it to the enemy or not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House has just given first reading to a bill designed to patriate the Canadian constitution. That ought to remind us that one of the factors which motivated the Fathers of Confederation in bringing together the various provinces which now make up Canada was the fear that Canada would be overwhelmed and absorbed by the emerging giant to the south of us. 1 submit that this is still one of our major concerns. In the years which have transpired since 1867 we have gone a long way toward economic absorption, social assimilation, and political domination by the United States.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), in the policy paper which he presented to the New Democratic Party council- about which he has spoken in this House-called "An Industrial Strategy for Canada", contended that economic growth in Canada depends upon retaining our valuable resources under Canadian ownership and control.
The Liberal party in Canada has always paid lip service to the idea of maintaining economic independence for this country. Many members who have sat in the House in the Liberal ranks over the last 15 years have been members of the committee for an independent Canada, but the fact is that the record of their performance with respect to maintaining Canada as an independent economic entity has been a dismal one.
The present government has been in office for 15 years. In 1963, headed by Walter Gordon, Donald Macdonald, and Judy LaMarsh, a group came marching into the House of Commons to the tune of "Oh Canada, we stand on guard for thee". However, in the years which followed there was no change with respect to the steady encroachment upon our economic independence by large United States controlled multinational corporations. Then in the election campaign of 1974 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a commitment to the people of this country. This is what he said:
The Liberal Party of Canada sets as an objective that major new projects in the natural resource field should have at least 50 per cent, and preferably 60 per cent, Canadian equity ownership.
I asked the Prime Minister yesterday if that commitment still stood, and the Prime Minister answered in the affirmative. All the facts prove him to be wrong and, if he were on to his job, he would know that he was wrong. For instance, if he takes a look at the long list of oil and gas companies which have been taken over by foreign corporations since June, 1974,

June 20, 1978
Natural Resources
he will realize that the 50 per cent to 60 per cent Canadian ownership clause has not been applied. If he takes the trouble to look at the figures which were put out by corporations under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, he will find that in the last year for which figures are available, which was 1975, of foreign companies in the petroleum and coal products field foreign ownership is 95 per cent in equity, 95 per cent in sales, and 95 per cent in profits.
However, 1 think probably the most damning indictment of the Prime Minister's failure to uphold his commitment to maintain 50 per cent to 60 per cent Canadian ownership is to be found in the document I hold in my hand, which is a copy of a document over the signature of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner). It is a review of the matter of Canadian ownership compared with foreign ownership in this country. It shows, in the first place, that consistently there have been takeovers by foreign corporations which have not involved 50 per cent Canadian ownership. The document says that in most instances so far it has not proven feasible to secure full compliance with the objective of Canadian ownership of resource-based companies. The Prime Minister put forward this policy in June, 1974. He said yesterday that it still stands, but the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce says that it has not been found feasible to put it into effect. Who is telling the truth, the Prime Minister or the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce?
In this document the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce admits that most investors know very little about this policy. He says, and I quote:
-at present many, perhaps most, foreign investors are not aware of this policy objective. There has been very little publicity and the last statement on the subject is three years old.
In this same document the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce suggests the advisability of dropping this provision, but he adds that the public should not be told about it because, and again I quote:
-it would be preferable that there be no public statement to that effect so as to minimize the danger that the change of practice would be seen as a fall-back by the government.
The government's commitment to maintain 50 per cent to 60 per cent Canadian ownership has proved to be a farce. The government has proved that it has not seriously attempted to carry out its policy or to maintain the level to which the Prime Minister committed his government in 1974. I know of no better illustration of this than the oil industry, which is the best example of creeping economic continentalism and the growing U.S. domination of our resource industries.
In the last 50 years the control of light oil in this country has been taken over almost entirely by U.S. majors. Virtually 100 per cent of the light crude oil in this country is now under the control of U.S. petroleum companies. The result is that they have raped this resource to the point where we have only about ten years' supply left. Sixty per cent of our production of oil and natural gas for years went to the U.S., even though it

was well known that the amount of reserves, we had on hand was perilously low.
Now that we have only ten years' supply left, the industry began to look at other sources. The next area it looked at was the tar sands. One might have thought that we would have learned from the light oil experience, and that there would have been some public participation or Canadian ownership in the development of the tar sands. But no, we allowed the three large U.S. companies which form Syncrude not only to take over the development of a large area of the tar sands but to do so with the financial assistance of the Government of Canada and of the governments of Ontario and Alberta. As a matter of fact the Canadian people are putting up a major part of the money in return for a minor interest in that development, and it is interesting that the next company in line is the Shell Oil Company, another U.S. company which is going to develop the tar sands.
That brings us to the present situation when we find that the only remaining oil acreage we have in this country which is not completely under foreign domination is the heavy oil deposits on the Saskatchewan-Alberta border. These oil deposits may be very important for the future industrial development of Canada, because at present we see from the 1977 figures that Canada has a net deficit in oil production of approximately 100,000 barrels a day. The result is that in 1977 we had a deficit, as a result of imported oil, of $1.5 billion, and with our exports being phased out because of our diminishing reserves it is estimated that by 1985 our deficit could reach $5 billion. In light of that fact, the heavy oil acreage in western Canada becomes of tremendous importance. That area is largely controlled by the Husky Oil Company which has over 1.5 million acres under lease or under option. It is estimated that with the new technology now available, it has 16 billion barrels of recoverable oil.
Joseph Baird, the president of Occidental Oil, is reported in this morning's paper as having said, "This is a real carrot". Yes, 16 billion barrels of recoverable oil in a good area, reasonably accessible, not like oil in the Arctic or in the ocean, but a supply of oil which would meet Canada's needs and save us from being importers of oil and from becoming increasingly dependent upon the oil producing countries which at present have such tremendous power around the world, is a real carrot.
For over a year Petro-Canada has been endeavouring to persuade Husky to begin a large scale development of this heavy oil, but no action has taken place. I am told that it even offered a partnership to help them raise the necessary capital, but that was not acceptable. As a matter of fact I suspect that the oil industry is not averse to having Canada find it necessary to import some of its oil, particularly if they buy that oil from sources which the multinational oil companies control. Finally, Petro-Canada did what seemed to me was the logical thing to do. It made an offer to purchase the Husky Oil Company and to develop that field, either alone or in partnership with the Saskatchewan and Alberta governments, and I want to point out that they did so with the approval of the
June 20, 1978

cabinet, as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) has stated in the House.
This was a logical step to take, but what do we find? We find that whereas on Monday, June 20, as reported at page 6268 of Hansard, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that this development by Petro-Canada of the heavy oil deposits was "in the national interest", by the end of the week the picture began to change. We see it, first of all, in the words of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who criticized the decision made by Petro-Canada, and when Occidental made counter offers to Petro-Canada's offer to buy Husky, he said, "I'm not shedding many tears over Petro-Canada", and Alberta's energy minister, Don Getty, said on television the other night that they "don't want a publicly owned company" in the field.

speechtext: Nor does Canada, if it is based on your Saskatchewan government's policies!

I see this is endorsed by some of the Progressive Conservative members who share that view.
I want to remind the House that the U.S. and Canada are probably the only two industrialized nations in the world that do not have a publicly owned oil company which controls the major part of the oil industry in their countries.
The gentlemen to my right might hold back the forces of progress for a while, but the fact is that eventually the Canadian people will insist on having a voice in determining the development of their own resources.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Last
Thursday, as reported at page 6432 of Hansard, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources had changed his mind and said that it was no longer "in the public interest" for Petro-Canada to develop the Husky Oil acreage. He then took the position that it was in the national interest that the oil deposits be developed, irrespective of who develops them. That is quite a switch. He went on to say further that if it were guaranteed that Occidental would develop the field, then the Canadian objective would have been achieved. That change of pace in two days is difficult to understand. First of all, it was a clear signal to FIR A that there would be no objection from the cabinet if FIRA decided to allow the transfer of the Husky Oil assets to Occidental which is bidding against Petro-Canada. But I ask, what kind of sellout are we witnessing?
Natural Resources
Why was Petro-Canada bidding for Husky Oil in the first place if it is not important that Petro-Canada develop this oilfield, and if Occidental is now interested in developing that field, what has Occidental been doing until now when Petro-Canada and the government were trying to find some person or persons to develop that field? The result is that Petro-Canada has become the birdie in sort of a badminton game between two American companies, which are bouncing it back and forth. Every time Petro-Canada makes a bid, Occidental tops it. I ask the House to consider what this does to the status of Petro-Canada in this country and the international petroleum business. The government's treatment of Petro-Canada, in saying that it does not matter who develops the field so long as it is developed, demeans Petro-Canada. The cabinet is demeaning itself by making it appear to all the world that it is manipulated by the oil cartel, which has been calling the tune up until now, and apparently is still doing so.
This topic is very important because a great deposit of oil either will be developed by Canadians for Canadians, or it will pass into the control of a foreign corporation over which we will have little control. If the government was not able to persuade Husky to develop the field with sufficient urgency, we have no guarantee that Occidental will develop the field with sufficient urgency to meet the oil needs of Canada.
The first line of defence is FIRA. It has the power to recommend that there be no transfer from Husky to Occidental, or to recommend that the transfer be permitted. Up until now, in my opinion, FIRA has been a comparatively toothless tiger. It has allowed transfer after transfer, although the memo of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce showed that there was not 50 per cent Canadian ownership. This time FIRA has a chance to redeem itself. My hope is that it will be seized of the importance to Canada of applying the 50 per cent to 60 per cent Canadian ownership commitment and insist that no transfer be permitted.
Our second line of defence is the cabinet. They are the body who must make the final decision on the basis of a recommendation from FIRA. I am not overly optimistic. Certainly the cabinet has not been very diligent in applying the 50 per cent to 60 per cent rule which was set forth by the Prime Minister in June, 1974. I hope public opinion in this country will be so aroused that pressure will be brought upon cabinet to apply the 50 per cent to 60 per cent ownership provision, and to say that the development of heavy oil deposits on the Alberta-Sas-katchewan border will not be transferred to the Occidental Oil Company, but that they will be developed by the people's own company, Petro-Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: In closing, what makes a nation great is not just its constitution. A constitution is an attempt to put into legal form the hopes, aspirations, and objectives of free people. A nation only becomes great when that nation has a sense of pride and purpose. It cannot have that if its resources are to be owned outside its own borders, and if it is to have no voice whatsoever in the determination of its own economic destiny.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
The
Canadian historian, Frank Underhill, whom many of us remember with admiration and affection, once said that a nation is a collection of people who have done great things together in the past and who are determined to do great things together in the future. Canadians have done great things in the

past. There is a long litany of accomplishments in peace and in war of which we can be proud. Nothing would do more to galvanize Canadians and make us a great nation than to have a sense of purpose in respect of developing our own resources, to do it with our own money and our own effort, and to be the arbiters of our own destiny. In order to do those things we need courageous leadership, and an opportunity to develop our resources. Neither the leadership nor the opportunity has been given to us by the government. If the government and the House fail to deal courageously with this problem, then we and those who come after us will have to pay the price of our inertia and apathy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members present will be glad to know that I do not intend to take up my full allotment of time in respect of this matter, simply because we do not think there is enough merit in the concept indicated by the New Democratic motion today to take up too much of the time of the House. This is not to say that we disagree with everything in the motion by any means, nor do we disagree with all the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas).
In this House, in the political field of this country, and as far as public opinion is concerned, nationalistic sentiment is not solely the prerogative of the New Democratic Party, the Liberal party or the Progressive Conservative party by any means. Certainly, for one, I agree it is long past due when Canada's national resources should be developed by and for the Canadian national interest. But in many respects we certainly do not agree with the nationalistic sentiments expressed by the hon. member who was the mover of the motion and who has just sat down.
Contrary, however, to the merits of his argument, and contrary to the main thrust of the socialistic dogma to which he adheres, and from which, unfortunately, there is no difference in concept, principle or policy on the part of the federal Liberal government of the day, we emphatically do not believe, as the hon. member just indicated, that there are only two choices or two alternatives.
That hon. member said there are only two alternatives. One of those alternatives, in his mind, obviously is the continued domination of the Canadian oil industry by foreigners, and perhaps even a consolidation through the offer or the bid by the Occidental Oil Company of California to take over Husky Oil of Canada. That is the one choice the hon. member graphically describes for us. That is not his choice, that is not my choice, and it is not our party's choice.
The other alternative he presented to the House and the public, however, as the only way Canadian resources can be preserved for Canadian use and, in the long term, for the Canadian national interest, is to have a Canadian federal governmental agency take it over.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
June 20, 1978

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Obviously the applause from the NDP benches for that type of program comes as no surprise. What was surprising, however, was that from the federal Liberal benches during the course of the remarks by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, there was equal applause for some of those sentiments respecting a governmental Crown agency. The minister of the day nodded his head and grinned, indicating that is perfectly correct.
Those two are not the only alternatives; they are not the only choices, no matter how much the socialists and near socialists believe those are the choices to be presented to the Canadian people.
There is another choice, and that other choice is obviously far preferable, not only in the short run but in the long-term interests of the development of Canadian resources by and for Canadians, and that other choice has to be, and it should be our position, that Husky Oil and the development of the heavy oil fields be undertaken by Canadian interests, by Canadians through the Canadian private sector, not the Canadian public sector.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I suggest that is completely distinct from the position taken by the hon. member who has just sat down, for the NDP socialists, and completely distinct from the position which I know the minister has taken, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) undoubtedly has taken through this whole sorry mess which has led us to this situation today. That position has been that the only answer has to be Petro-Can or a Canadian government agency bidding for the shares of Husky. 1 say we disagree profoundly with the principle that a federal governmental agency is the only answer to Canadian control of Canadian resources. Specifically in relation to this matter, we believe that Petro-Can should not control the Canadian development of heavy oil in this country.
Our position is that Canadian private interests can and should be encouraged to develop Canadian resources, and the very obvious and determined present national federal government policy and concept, directed right out of the Prime Minister's office, has been and still is to discourage any other development but that of Petro-Can. We think this is wrong, that it is folly, that it is unfair and highly discriminatory, and it certainly can never serve the Canadian long-term interests either in heavy oil, energy generally or, for that matter, in the Canadian resources field generally.
Heavy oil development has not proceeded as it should have, and there are many reasons for this. We just heard the argument presented to us, and the socialists and the Liberals of this country both claim this, that it is the fault of foreign, specifically American, management and control of the present land-the present land owners, in particular, Husky Oil of Canada. Husky Oil of Canada at the moment is obviously controlled by foreign interests-by American interests. We believe it takes at least two to tango.
Natural Resources
Our enquiries, and I have reason to believe they have a very great modicum of authority, have led us to believe there certainly has been a concept and plan, emanating from the very top of our present federal government, which have brought home to Husky over a period of the last three months, in no uncertain terms, that come hell or high water this present federal government is going to permit only Petro-Can to develop the heavy oil potential. We say this is wrong, heavy handed, and discriminatory. It is against our concept of what Petro-Can was set up for in the first place, and it is against the long-term interests of Canada.
How many more federal government agencies will be required to bail out, take over, or buy back some of these fields when they come on market? Are we forever going to be required to rely on the half knowledge of federal governmental people, in particular of persons in the federal government at the political level, in taking over these fields as they may become available in the future?
I agree completely that control should not have passed from Canada in the first place, and perhaps that is a damning indictment not only of this government but of all past governments. In any event, it has happened, and it has happened by a number of ways and means which can be directly related to the policies and principles of successive federal governments, not only in the energy field and not only in the resources field, but also in the tax field. There is no question about that. Nevertheless, it has happened, and the facts speak for themselves.
The Canadian resources industry generally is dominated by foreigners. The Canadian energy field industries are dominated by foreigners, and the Canadian petroleum industry is dominated by foreigners. However, do you really think it is the government of the day that we should continually be looking to in order to bail us out of the situation we are in as a result of these past errors and failures? God forbid! I do not care what the political complexion is of the government of the day. This is a wrong, heavy-handed move. If I had my "druthers", for instance, not only would I move specifically to make sure that that the Occidental bid was never countenanced by the government of the day, but I would also move to make very sure that the Petro-Canada bid was withdrawn as well. It is a wrong move to encourage, and it is wrong to use a heavy hand, as this government has been using over the last few months, to discourage and to drag its feet in respect of that heavy oil development.
The heavy oil development should have been well on its way by now, but it is not. It is not the fault of foreigners but of the footdragging of this government and its numerous agencies in the field. Husky Oil has known for some time, and let us make no bones about it, that they were not going to be permitted under this government to develop that heavy oil field. There is no question about that whatsoever.
The hon. member spoke the other day of collusion between Occidental Oil and Husky Oil, and that may well be the case.

It has been destroyed by successive counter offers made by companies which may not really be in the game on the one hand, and a governmental agency on the other hand which feels it has no restriction or limitation whatsoever on the amount of money it can pay. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what new oil resources are going to be available to the people of Canada that we do not know about now? What new development, what real initiative and leadership are taking place that will bring new wealth and new industry to Canada as a whole? What is going to happen to that $500 million to $800 million that will be spent under this scheme, which was devised in the Prime Minister's office and encouraged by the socialists on our left, those socialists who like to wrap themselves in the flag and indicate what great patriots and nationalists they are? I will tell you what is going to happen, Mr. Speaker. Under this scheme that $800 million of Canadian taxpayers' funds are going to travel south of the border. What good, Mr. Speaker, is that money going to do Canada when it crosses the border? What new development is that going to foster in this country? Absolutely none!
The minister is about to speak when I sit down, and I hope he will give us a lot more detail than has been provided so far. This is not the sole and exclusive policy of a governmental Crown agency that we are talking about when we talk of Petro-Canada and its two offers so far; we are talking about a policy that has been devised and initiated not even, I suspect, in the offices of the hon. ministers but in the office of the Prime Minister of this country. There are many, many close connections between what has happened over the last four months and individuals who deal with and have connections with the Prime Minister's office itself.
We on this side of the House suspect that a concerted, intentional, and prejudicial series of moves have been put into play on Husky in order to get it out of the picture and to make sure that everyone else is scared off due to some of the unreal statements and offers that have been made. If the Petro-Canada offer is so closely connected with the policies and principles of this government, I hope that the minister of the day will tell us what the basis of the Petro-Can offer is. How do they arrive at the figure which they have just come along with, because this is not his money or Petro-Can's money; this is the money of the people of this country? It is a very high trust, and burden, placed on the minister of the Crown responsible for this agency to the people of this country.
1 would like a very detailed explanation. Why is it $58; why is it not $78; why is it not $38? How are these things devised. I hope we are going to get an explanation, because it is owed to us in view of the fact this government is spending the taxpayers' money. 1 am also looking for an explanation of the great volume of share selling and buying and the activity that occurred prior to the public announcement of Petro-Canada's offer. Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate this afternoon which addresses itself to two very important issues. The first issue is that of Canadian ownership and control of resource developments in Canada, and the second issue, the current one, is whether development of Husky's heavy oil resources should be undertaken by Petro-Canada in co-operation with the provinces directly affected.
1 listened to the speech of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) with great interest and care. This is an area with which 1 was associated in my previous portfolio and with which I am very much involved in my present porfolio. I should like to tell the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that 1 thought he made a very good speech but, of course, that does not mean I agree with everything he said. Many of us on this side of the House could agree with the sentiments he uttered today and the degree to which he put Canada first in his remarks.
By contrast, I was appalled when the official spokesman for the Conservative party, the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), said he was not going to take all the time allotted to him today-although he was able to, with our encouragement. I think it is appalling when the official spokesman for the official party-the party that would like to become the government of this country-

-says that he is not going to take all his time to address himself to this issue because in some way this issue is not important to him or his party. That is a shocking situation. Clearly the Conservative party is retreating once again in a major policy area. They are running away from responsibility; they are hiding their heads because they do not want to state their position. 1 have heard comments to the effect that they may not have one. That is probably the kindest thing we could say. There is so much contention within the party that they cannot make up their minds.
I could not but reflect upon a phrase the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham used. I think his words were to the effect that we should bail ourselves out of past errors. I could not think of a better description of the mandate he was given by his own party in this House-"to bail us out of our past errors." Quite clearly their past error is that they are still living with it and do not know what to do with it. That error was that they voted against the creation of Petro-Canada.
I was appalled that the energy spokesman of the official opposition was not prepared to address himself to the question of energy policy. We on this side of the House would have liked to hear what the Conservatives have to say. I think a lot of people in the country have been wondering for a long time what the position of the Tory party is on energy.
In my opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, I referred to the two parts of this resolution. 1 should like to deal briefly with a review of the policy initiatives, the legislative action, regulato-
Natural Resources
ry action, and legislative proposals of this government in the last four years.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands referred to FIRA. This legislation was originally passed by the House in 1973. Part I was proclaimed in the early part of 1974, but part II was not proclaimed until this parliament. The Foreign Investment Review Agency was a very significant piece of legislation in the development of Canadian policy for the development and protection of Canadian resources. Hon. members are aware of the one test contained in the Foreign Investment Review Agency Act, the phrase "significant benefit to Canada". The act was not set up to block foreign investment unless that investment does not provide significant benefit to Canada.
The second significant event 1 should like to refer to was also referred by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, and that is the election promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the Sault in the late spring of 1974. When I was minister of industry, trade and commerce I referred to that promise as reported in the Commons Debates for October 10, 1974, when I said:
The Prime Minister said that the Liberal Party of Canada sets as its objective that new, major projects in the natural resources field should have at least 50 per cent, and preferably 60 per cent, Canadian equity ownership. As there are overlapping responsibilities for the development of Canada's natural resources shared by both the federal government and the provinces, he said we would hope to pursue this objective jointly with the provinces.
I will return later in my remarks to the part the provinces might and should play in this area of ownership and the question of the percentage of Canadian equity participation.
Yesterday the Prime Minister was asked whether he stood by that statement, and he replied very quickly that he does. That was an important statement in 1974, and that was an important statement yesterday.
Perhaps I might refer in passing, Mr. Speaker, to that statement about 50 per cent and preferably 60 per cent Canadian equity ownership, which today is seen as part of that policy in respect of resources. One can think back to the government of the day and the policy with respect to uranium in this country-that Canadians should hold 67 per cent of all new projects. In a few moments I will refer to the oil and gas bill now before the House which takes the same kinds of proposals a step further in that industry. The result of that uranium policy was to ensure that a project at Key Lake, Saskatchewan, will be Canadian controlled. More than that, a Canadian Crown corporation, Eldorado, will participate in that project because Inexco, the American corporation which was a one third partner in the deal, decided it would sell its ownership. It provided an option to Eldorado, which in turn has set up one half of that development to the Saskatchewan government. As a result of that, there will be greater Canadian participation in the uranium industry.
The next significant event in this parliament was the passage of the Petro-Canada Act in July, 1975. It is worth

quoting for the record and for the edification of members of the official opposition the purposes of the act:
The purpose of this Act is to establish within the energy industries in Canada a Crown owned company with authority to explore for hydrocarbon deposits, to negotiate for and acquire petroleum and petroleum products from abroad to assure a continuity of supply for the needs of Canada, to develop and exploit deposits of hydrocarbons within and without Canada in the interests of Canada, to carry out research and development projects in relation to hydrocarbons and other fuels, and to engage in exploration for, and the production, distribution, refining and marketing of, fuels.
About a week ago another member of the official opposition, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), raised a question during question period which suggested that the Crown corporation, Petro-Canada, did not have a mandate for the acquisition of other companies. I draw his attention to the objectives, powers and duties set forth in the Petro-Canada Act. 1 quote paragraph 6:
The objects of the Corporation are
(a)	to engage in exploration for and the development of hydrocarbons and other types of fuel or energy;
(b)	to engage in research and development projects relating to fuel and energy resources;
(c)	to import, produce, transport, distribute, refine and market hydrocarbons of all descriptions;
(d)	to produce, distribute, transport and market other fuels and energy; and
(e)	to engage or invest in ventures or enterprises related to the exploration, production, importation, distribution, refining and marketing of fuel, energy and related resources.
The mandate of Petro-Canada is very clear in this area, although the official opposition may not be very clear about it.
On July 18, 1975, the government promulgated a new set of principles for international business conduct. It might be worth referring to those principles because they have not received the attention they deserve. These principles in July, 1975, served notice on companies doing business in Canada that there were certain expectations which the government had with regard to their conduct. 1 quote the preamble:
Foreign-controlled businesses in Canada are expected to operate in ways that will bring significant benefit to Canada. To this end they should pursue policies that will foster their independence in decision-making, their innovative and other entrepreneurial capabilities, their efficiency, and their identification with Canada and the aspirations of the Canadian people.
There are 14 separate principles set out. 1 wish to refer to Nos. 1 and 9. The first one reads:
Pursue a high degree of autonomy in the exercise of decision-making and risk-taking functions, including innovative activity and the marketing of any resulting new products.
Number 9 reads:
Create a financial structure that provides opportunity for substantial equity participation in the Canadian enterprise by the Canadian public.
The next move that was taken was a year ago in August. This is a significant one. Again there has been very little reference to it by the official opposition. I refer to the new regulations that were established for the exploration and development of oil and gas on federal lands. There were three particular principles which were set out at that time and which are now operative.

The first one provides a preference for Petro-Canada with regard to Crown lands. We gave Petro-Canada an option to look over the then existing Crown lands which were not out to permit or to lease, and to choose from those lands 25 per cent.
The second preference was that Petro-Canada could select up to 25 per cent of any lands surrendered back to the Crown by other oil companies. This is over a period of seven years following promulgation of the regulations. In those two ways regulations have been made to give Petro-Canada a preference in the development of Crown land under federal control.
The third regulation promulgated at that time had to do with the back-in provision for Petro-Canada when a permit came up for special renewal. This special renewal is not an automatic decision on the part of the administrative authority. It is a discretionary one.
The government at that time introduced a back-in provision which in effect stated that if there is no more than 10 per cent Canadian ownership in a particular project, Petro-Canada would have a 25 per cent right to back in and then pay its way from then on in. If there is 35 per cent Canadian participation in a project, Petro-Canada would not have any right to back in.
There was a heavy emphasis on getting Canadian ownership into that particular phase of the exploration cycle. If Canadian ownership was already there, Petro-Canada had no right up to 35 per cent. However, between 10 and 35 per cent the Crown corporation would have special rights.
In January, 1976, Petro-Canada started up. In August, 1976, it acquired the assets of ARCAN, which was the Atlantic Richfield subsidiary operating in Canada. As hon. members will recall, that corporation was not able to hack it with the Syncrude project. It was the withdrawal of ARCAN which created the condition of near disaster for that project, and the governments of Alberta and Ontario, as well as the federal government, had to move in to salvage this project for the benefit of Canada.
The assets were acquired in August, 1976, by Petro-Canada. 1 do not recall the official opposition raising any objection at that time. If they did, I am surprised that they did not remind us today. It is another clear example of the inconsistencies and inability of the official opposition really to decide how they are going to treat the Crown corporation.

June 20, 1978

In conclusion, with regard to the foreign investment side, I believe that any fair minded person will have to say that the record shows a very strong commitment on the part of the government to increasing Canadian participation and control in Canadian resource development. These measures have been taken during the life of this parliament, over the past four years. We have seen no comparable commitment to these issues by the official opposition.
The official position of the official opposition is that they would dismantle Petro-Canada if they were to form the next government. They would rely more on the national oil companies of other countries than they would on the national oil company of Canada. They seem to have forgotten that a national oil company, British Petroleum, operates in Canada. They seem to have forgotten that the French government has a national oil company investing in Canada. The official opposition seem to have forgotten that the Italian government has a national oil company operating in Canada. They have forgotten that the German government has an investment in the oil and gas industry in this country. They have forgotten that the Japanese government has an investment in this country. What they are saying to the Canadian people is that they are quite prepared to accept the national oil companies of other countries, but they are not prepared to accept our own national oil company. 1 think it is about time members of the Conservative party moved into the twentieth century because the position they have taken on this issue is to return to the colonization approach, the colonial attitude of their heyday.
I should like to turn, now, to the subject of the development of heavy oil in Saskatchewan in the context of our policy of self-reliance for Canada. It is important that hon. members should recognize that this policy of reducing our dependence on foreign oil was endorsed by the provincial premiers at the first ministers' conference in February. Moreover, the heavy oil of Saskatchewan was singled out for special treatment by the premiers, including the premier of Saskatchewan, presumably.
Hon. members will realize how important the heavy oil resources of Canada are if they have referred recently to a booklet put out by my department "Oil Sands and Heavy Oils-the Prospects." I would refer them to page three which sets out the proportion of oil sands which are available commercially, the economic possibilities, and attraction to investors. In the Lloydminster area alone these deposits are the equivalent of about half the recoverable reserves in the conventional fields of Alberta. That is how important they are.
The corporate sector, more particularly Husky, has its own time frame from the point of view of the development of company assets. We are dealing here with a classic situation in which the legitimate time frame of the private sector does not conform with the time frame which the government has determined to be in the national interest. Petro-Canada, along with the government of Saskatchewan, the federal government and Husky, held a number of discussions about the development of
Natural Resources
these sands. It was the view of Petro-Canada that it would not be possible, given the sense of urgency attached to the matter by the Government of Canada, to reach a solution without making a take-over bid. This bid, together with the counter bid by Occidental and the further bid by Petro-Canada, is now history, and time alone will tell what the result will be. But I believe Canadians can feel reassured by the presence of the Foreign Investment Review Act. Occidental has already noted the importance of that legislation and made its offer conditional not just upon the basis of 80 per cent acceptance but on the basis of its approval under the act. The corporation has also stated it wants Petro-Canada along with it. Petro-Canada, for its part, has announced that it is preparing its own offer.
The other main conclusion we might draw at this time reflecting on both issues, this project and the Canadian development of resources, particularly the ownership criteria which might apply, is that the provinces have remained silent for too long. It is up to the provinces, now, to accept the Prime Minister's invitation to discuss this question of 50 per cent, preferably 60 per cent, Canadian equity ownership of resource projects. Too much time has gone by. There seems to be too much emphasis on the part of the provinces on questions having to do with their jurisdiction and ownership of the resources. It is time to let Canadians know what share of the equity participation Canadians should enjoy in major new projects.
The time has come for the Tories to address themselves to this question, too. We know how they stand with regard to Petro-Canada. They would dismantle it. This may be a very uneasy policy position for them to live with. I would welcome a change of mind on their part; it is long overdue. But I would welcome it if they would address their attention to this question of Canadian participation. The hon. member for North-umberland-Durham talked about straw men. He never once dealt with the question of what his party believed to be a reasonable degree of participation of Canadians in the resource development of our country.
The people know where the Liberals stand; our record in this parliament is clear. I think the time has come to hear from the official opposition. Canadians would also welcome a statement from the provincial premiers.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) for having moved this motion.
Last week, the hon. member proved his awareness of the problem by raising this issue several times in questions put to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie). Though he did not obtain all the explanations he sought, he still made the House more aware than before of this serious problem.

June 20, 1978
Natural Resources
Mr. Speaker, the Husky Oil affair underlines once more the need for Canadians to control their natural resources. At the federal-provincial conference of the ministers of energy last year, one of the items on the agenda was the problem of heavy oil development. The final paper stated that it would cost from $3 to $5 a barrel to convert this heavy oil into useful resources on a large scale. The development of heavy oil therefore requires large investments. According to the Saskatchewan premier, Husky Oil alone cannot support the cost of building a plant for this purpose. Last Wednesday, he estimated the cost of developing the Husky Oil supplies and of building a heavy oil extraction plant at about $2 billion. Heavy oil reserves on the Saskatchewan-Alberta boundary are evaluated at five billion barrels. This may not seem a lot if we think about the estimated supplies of 900 billion barrels in the Alberta tar sands. But extracting oil from the tar sands also involves certain problems. In the case of Husky Oil, you would simply have to inject hot water, in other words use a thermal process, to help the flow of the oil which is too heavy. This development therefore involves only a technological problem since the capital is virtually assured following the offers of Petro-Canada and Occidental. Last June 15, I was listening to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who replied to my colleague for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that whoever the final owner of the Husky Company may be, what counts is that these resources be developed and that they be developed in the national interest.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that when we have a Canadian company, publicly owned to boot, which wants to purchase an oil company which on its own cannot develop oil deposits for the benefit of Canadians, we cannot sit quietly by and let an American company take the development of our energy resources which are vital for the progress of our economy. National interest does not call only for the resources to be developed for Canadians, but also for these resources to be developed by Canadians. The interference of a foreign company in this shameful bargaining has inflated the market value of Husky Oil shares to such a point that Petro-Canada had to raise its offer to $52 a share last week. Frankly I wonder if the Occidental company from California, which indulges in such a financial scheme, deserves our confidence since that increase in value of the stock will result in higher costs and eventually all Canadians will have to pay for it through government subsidies or a price increase. The rich will get even richer at the expense of others.
Mr. Speaker, let us not forget that the large majority of our resource companies are under foreign control. In certain circumstances a Canadian company can be taken over by an American company because there is no Canadian company to buy it. But in the present circumstances, a bid has been filed by a Canadian corporation-Petro-Canada which is owned by all Canadians-to purchase another Canadian corporation.

Then, Mr. Speaker, in light of the financial bargaining that forced Petro-Canada to increase its initial offer of $45 a share to $52 to control Husky Oil, only to see Occidental offer $55 a share, I simply believe that our interests are far from being protected. Petro-Canada will have no control over the development of those important resources. I know that Occidental propose that Petro-Canada participate in a consortium to develop heavy oils in Lloydminster and acquire a third of the shares in the development of those deposits. But who will get control over those deposits? Foreign interests.
Then, Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told us during the last election that all major new resource developments should be Canadian controlled, was he joking or did he only try to fool Canadians? The fact is that Petro-Canada has been had by a foreign company. The Foreign Investment Review Agency might accept the proposals of Occidental and authorize it to take over Husky Oil. Where are we going? When will Canadians have a word to say about the control and development of our resources?
Mr. Speaker, our natural resources are not the only things under foreign control, there is also our economy where at least 90 per cent of business is controlled by foreigners, who are often our nearest neighbours, our neighbours to the south. The commitments made by the Prime Minister during the 1974 election have been forgotten to the extent that the government itself is prepared to surrender our birthrights to foreigners against a mess of pottage. Mr. Speaker, this is the work of a government which has had the majority for almost four years.

Mr. Speaker, as I start off in this debate I must correct the minister, who again has misinformed the House. I cannot say whether it was intentional or through ignorance, but following the earlier example of my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) with regard to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) I will concede that it was probably the latter.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) claimed that we were inaccurate in describing the mandate of Petro-Canada. I refer the minister to a document put out by his predecessor called "An Energy Policy for Canada", published in early July of 1973, in which is contained an analysis of the worth of a national oil company. The analysis contained arguments for a national oil company and arguments against. Anyone reading these arguments without any built-in bias would come to the conclusion that there was not a good argument for a national oil company. The argument against was not strongly against, but on the basis of the analysis done by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources of the Liberal government under the hon. Donald Macdonald, who was then the minister, one would come to that conclusion.
However, in the fall of 1973 and in 1974, because of the Middle East war the OPEC nations gained strength, and there
June 20, 1978

were fears about shortages of oil in Canada. It was largely on the strength of the newfound realization that, as a country, we could not count on cheap foreign oil to supply our needs, that the government came to the conclusion that one of the vehicles to be used to improve Canada's security of supply would be a national oil company. That was the main reason for the establishment of Petro-Canada, in the face of the government's own analysis which indicated that such a national oil company would probably not be a good idea.
That was not very long ago, and the minister can check the record. If he wants to check the March 12, 1975, issue of Hansard, he will see a speech by his predecessor indicating that in order to promote more security of energy supply for Canada the government was establishing a national oil company to be called Petro-Canada. The original mandate of Petro-Canada when the act was written-and it was written like all acts are written by this government, with a huge, broad brush-was to make sure Petro-Canada could do anything, including pumping gas and changing tires, if that was deemed to be in the national interest. So the act indeed empowers Petro-Canada to do anything. No one ever claimed that what Petro-Canada was doing in trying to take over Husky is in contravention of the act. But it is certainly not in keeping with the original reason given by this government for the establishment of Petro-Canada.
Then, to bolster his argument, the minister brought in the question of the northern regulations establishing the rules which will prevail for exploration of federal lands in the high Arctic. I am appalled that he could use that argument. He said what a great thing it was that Petro-Canada had this favoured position. As the minister should be aware, since the promulgation of those regulations the private sector has abandoned federal lands in the high Arctic and there is virtually no exploration occurring up there, other than that which is captive, namely, PanArctic, with Petro-Canada being the owner of 45 per cent of it.

speechtext: The minister thinks that the north is everything north of Toronto.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
The net result of the minister's regulations, for which he takes credit, is the cessation of exploration in Canada's Arctic. How that will help us achieve self-sufficiency or self-reliance is beyond me. Apparently what the government has done, without admitting it to the Canadian people, is to abandon the notion of self-sufficiency, the idea of Canada producing as much energy as it needs. The government is prepared to see Canadians rely on insecure offshore sources of oil and gas. If, heaven forbid, the day comes when those supplies are cut off and Canadians start freezing in the dark, the credit for that can go right to this minister and his government.
Questions are raised as to why we should dismantle Petro-Canada. There are lots of reasons, and I could debate this for a long time, but I will give just a few arguments based on the annual report of Petro-Canada for 1977. Some people may have seen press releases on Petro-Canada stating, for example,
Natural Resources
that Petro-Canada had $88 million in revenue in 1977, which is pure flimflam. It is true that their total revenues were $88 million, but you have to pay salaries and things like that, and when you take off expenses for salaries and rent, you get a revenue of $30 million, that is on assets of $878 million or equity of $551 million-$538 million at the start of the year.
In other words, the profit of that company before tax was 5.5 per cent on equity. The taxpayers put in $538 million, and the company did such a marvellous job of investing it that we got 5.5 per cent return on it, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is not in New York borrowing money at 9 per cent. It is a hell of a deal. We borrow at 9 per cent, give it to Petro-Canada, and then get 5.5 per cent on that. Then you wonder why we want to dismantle the company. By the way, the after tax return, which is what is really important, is 1.7 per cent on equity. In comparison, the average for the industry is in the vicinity of 17 per cent or 18 per cent, so Petro-Canada is doing one tenth as well as the average oil company in Canada. Small wonder! Who can expect any better?
We are talking about the same people who run the Post Office, for goodness sake. If they cannot deliver a letter, how the heck are they going to find oil and gas? Have they contributed to Canada's long term security supply? Let us look at the figures. They found 21 billion cubic feet of gas, but they sold 32 billion cubic feet, meaning they suffered a net depletion of 11 billion cubic feet of gas. They found 2.9 million barrels of oil, but they sold 10.2 million barrels of oil, meaning there was a net depletion of 7.3 million barrels of oil. So if you put a gas value on that in company terms, it comes out to $27 million of inventory that was sold. If you subtract that from the $30 million of net profit, you wind up with the large figure of $3 million on an investment of $538 million by the people of Canada. If that is not reason enough to dismantle the company, there are plenty of others.

The minister would like more reasons. Let him read the document produced by his own department back in 1973 and he will get lots of reasons there.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), who introduced the motion, ended his speech with the rhetorical question, what makes a nation great? He went on to state that it was a sense of purpose, a sense of pride, having goals and objectives, none of which I disagree with. It was well stated and nobody in this party would disagree with that. But then somehow, by some magic, he associated that directly with state ownership, with socialism. He said that the only way a nation can be great is if the state runs everything. That misses the fundamental elements of a nation, namely, the people.
It is the people, not bureaucracy, not government, that make a nation great. It is the releasing of the creative drive in people, the energy in individual Canadians who operate in a free economy where there are opportunities and where government is an assistance, not a hindrance by encouraging the growth of a huge, oppressive bureaucracy which the hon.

June 20, 1978

member is advocating. The effect of that can only be to stifle the individual and to prevent Canadians from taking on those activities which lead to greatness on an individual basis and as a nation.
Like my friend and colleague, the hon. member for North-umberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), I object most strenuously to the notion that only socialists are nationalists and patriots. I was a founding member of the committee for an independent Canada, and I believe that far too much of our economy is owned by foreigners. I know why that is so. It is because the oil industry is owned primarily by foreigners and it is because of the stupid tax laws in this country which have existed for too many years.
I do not know how many members in the House realize that until the budget of 1975 an American could invest in Canadian energy development on free tax dollars but a Canadian could not, so that we had the ludicrous situation where it was cheaper for an American to invest in Canada than for a Canadian to do so. That was the kind of tax law that existed in this country? Why? Because the Liberals, with the encouragement of the CCF and the NDP, wanted a tax system that gouged Canadians. They did not want incentive in the system so that Canadians could invest on an equal basis with foreigners in our own country.
When the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was the premier of Saskatchewan, he was not in Ottawa saying that he wanted to change the law so that Canadians could develop the oil reserves of Saskatchewan; he was inviting Husky to participate. Today the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands stood and sanctimoniously said that a true Canadian stands for more and more government and a state owned company to take over everything. Of all the sanctimonious-

Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broad-bent) stood and condemned the government's handling of the Post Office.
