speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my remarks by trying to reply to the last question of my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), who asked where the funds to finance such an undertaking would be coming from. For the information of my colleague, I would like to tell him that Canadians are indeed the most thrifty people in the world since they have the highest savings. In spite of a denigration campaign about everything that is Canadian, I am still confident that Canadians will recognize a good bargain when they see one and that they wil take the opportunity to make investments, not in a credit union or in a bank but in a Canadian business to develop the Canadian economy.
If Canadians do so, Mr. Speaker, they will be doing exactly like some twenty countries throughout the world. For example, allow me to point out that there are at least 25 French public agencies involved in mining operations in Canada. I will spare you, Mr. Speaker, the enumeration of the 25 organizations or agencies of the French government involved in Canada. There are also six German public agencies, five from the United Kingdom, five from Italy, two from the Netherlands, four from Japan and finally two from Spain, for a total of 45 government agencies of all those countries which have confidence in the Canadian economy and find it is excellent to invest and be involved in mining operations in Canada.
And it is that kind of astuteness, Mr. Speaker, to find such economic potential in Canada, which lacks in the provinces and which the provincial governments of Canada lack. The provinces' lack of enthusiasm is something scandalous, Mr. Speaker, because they do not contribute to the development of natural resources, especially of strategic resources like energy. It is this part of the excellent motion of my friend and distinguished colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) that I find the most important, that is the end of the second paragraph, paragraph (b), where he says, and I quote:
... the development of Husky Oil Company's heavy oil resources should be undertaken by Petro-Canada in co-operation with the provinces directly affected.
It is precisely, Mr. Speaker, because of this practically complete absence of contribution from the provinces in such undertakings, that so many foreign companies participate in them.
It is not surprising, Mr. Speaker, because it seems that anything coming from the Canadian government is depreciat-

ed, not only by persons whose interest is to depreciate our country, but also by several members of the opposition as well. And once again, one can see that Petro-Canada, which was established in spite of the opposition of the Progressive Conservative party, is a corporation which will guarantee all Canadians reliable energy resources, energy resources we can control. I do not understand the position of my colleague from Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) when he objects to the establishment or the development of Petro-Canada. Yet I did not hear any objection from him when his provincial government in Alberta nationalized Pacific Western Airlines. I wonder if the provincial government has made a mistake in launching such an undertaking. In his next speech, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member might let us know how he sees this action of the provincial government in the operation of an airline.
That is precisely the problem, Mr. Speaker. They are not consistent, they are not consistent with themselves. One day they have one policy, one way of doing things, and the next they have an entirely different way. But with this Liberal government, Mr. Speaker, it is always the same way. During a speech on the government's policy concerning the expansion of the industry and the development of natural resources which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) delivered in Sault Ste. Marie on June 28, 1974, he stated, and I quote:
The Liberal Party of Canada has set as its objective that new, major projects in the natural resources field should have at least 50 per cent, and preferably 60 per cent, Canadian equity ownership. As there are overlapping responsibilities for the development of Canada's natural resources shared by both the federal government and the provinces, the federal government hopes to pursue this objective jointly with the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, we know the provinces have always lagged behind; we have seen it happen in two easily identifiable undertakings, namely Petro-Canada and Syncrude. It was quite a job convincing the provinces to become involved and join the federal government. Later on during that same campaign, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) reaffirmed and dealt in depth with that policy objective in a statement to the House of Commons.
The Prime Minister stated in the House yesterday that that policy objective of the government had not changed. Contrary to what we often see our friends do across the way.
Everyone knows that foreign investments have played an extremely important part in the development of our natural resources in Canada and will continue to do so in the future. This influx of foreign capital in the past has resulted, among other things, in a large number of our resource industry in Canada belonging and being controlled today by foreign interests. Those industries are found predominantly in the sector of combustible minerals; they also assume a relatively important role in mining and forestry operations, and a comparatively small though not negligible one in the Canadian fishing sector.
However, there has been very little change in the level of foreign ownership in natural resources development industries.
June 20, 1978

The changes which actually took place over the last five years were aimed mainly at reducing the level of foreign ownership and raising the level of Canadian participation in these industries. The government has committed itself to promote higher Canadian participation and has passed a certain number of measures to that effect.
In 1970, the government adopted a policy limiting to 33 per cent the level of foreign ownership in uranium mining. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has stated that he will table a bill designed to implement this policy as soon as possible. Canadian participation in the development of petroleum and gas resources in the Arctic regions of Canada has been ensured by the direct involvement of the government in the PanArctic consortium.
Petro-Canada is a mechanism which we have created in spite of the Conservative opposition, as I indicated earlier, so that the federal government and Canadians generally could participate in the exploitation and the development of petroleum and gas resources of Canada.
Last year we amended the regulations governing petroleum and gas deposits in Canada in order to apply the policy which the government had already announced and whereby the authorization to produce crude oil from federal lands would be granted only if the enterprise had a Canadian financial involvement of at least 25 per cent. The government's commitment towards the increase of the Canadian content and participation in the development of resources has been reiterated in the document regarding the energy policy of the government entitled "An Energy Strategy for Canada". In keeping with the implementation of the Foreign Investments Review Act, we have paid particular attention to the government's objective concerning wider Canadian participation in natural resources development projects. Mr. Speaker, the results are quite eloquent.
Tremendous capital funds will be required for the expansion of natural resources industries in Canada in the next 10 or 12 years. In the area of energy alone, expenditures during the period from 1978 to 1990 should reach $188 billion. On the short run, capital expenditures in the field of energy should soar from $9.4 billion in 1977 to over $19 billion by 1982.
Foreign capital will obviously be required to support the Canadian economies if we are to reach the objective of selfsufficiency in energy and fully develop the important resources that exist in other sectors. Consequently, by pursuing its objective of boosting Canadian ownership in natural resources industries in Canada the government must take into consideration not only what is desirable but also what is achievable. Those claiming that Canadian resources should be exclusively developed by Canadians would unfortunately be postponing indefinitely a number of important projects which are now on the drafting board and which would create thousands and thousands of jobs for Canadians, contribute substantially to
Natural Resources
the correction of our balance of payments and stimulate considerably the Canadian economy as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, those are all reasons which prompt the government of Canada not to delay its involvement in the development of natural resources, more particularly energy resources. By doing that, Mr. Speaker, we are only showing as much managerial astuteness and skillfulness as those I named earlier, those seven or eight industrialized countries which chose to come and settle in Canada and contribute with Canadians to our economic development.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
This is a very important debate, Mr. Speaker, as has been pointed out by the other members who have preceded me. I think it is fair to say that it is fundamental to our continuing desire to achieve self-sufficiency in the supply of gas and oil for Canada's domestic needs. It brings up once again the important subject of ownership and control of our gas and oil resources in this country.
We in Canada may not have the luxury of ownership in this very important sector, but it is fair to say that we do have the opportunity to exercise control, and it is very important that we exercise that control, as we must and as we should. The important thing in this ongoing debate about the control and ownership of our natural resources is not so much a matter of whether we own them but, more important, a matter of whether we have the capability of controlling the manner in which these resources will be developed, that we have that capability at the federal and provincial levels and, to some extent, at the local levels.
It is also important that we put the whole question of the creation of Petro-Canada into its proper context. The minister took a great deal of his time today in his speech defending Petro-Canada, as he must, but we should be cognizant of the fact that the creation of Petro-Canada was not the result of de facto Liberal policy or philosophy; it was part and parcel of the Liberal survival package which was so important during those very difficult years they experienced between 1972 and 1974 when they had to call upon the support of the NDP to maintain power. When the NDP presented its so-called shopping list to the government as a condition of their support, the national oil company, which later became Petro-Canada, was an item on that list, and to be assured of their continuing support the government had to act upon that item. The Liberals buckled under the pressure of the NDP, and now this minister and this government are doing everything in their power to ensure that Petro-Canada becomes a viable participant in the oil industry in this country.
As I see it, the most important part of this debate is simply that the heavy oil reserves in the Lloydminster area must be developed. Indeed, it is important in the ongoing process of our attempt to achieve self-sufficiency and security of supply that this resource be developed. It is important too from a technological point of view because we are entering into an area in the development of the petrochemical industry where there is a
80045 -5OV2

June 20, 1978
Natural Resources
great deal of technical expertise yet to be developed. We are relatively elementary in that particular area because the heavy oil industry per se has not been looked upon over the years as a viable means by which we could achieve that goal of self-sufficiency, simply because heavy oil was used for other than traditional petroleum requirements. Essentially, heavy oil was used for asphalt paving, manufacturing of building materials, et cetera.
Development of the heavy oil reserves is important from an over-all economic point of view to Canada in terms of stimulating economic activity and of our desire to engage further in the processing and developing of our natural resources in secondary and tertiary ways. It is important furthermore that this resource be developed from the standpoint of Canada's endeavour to achieve an acceptable level in its balance of payments problem.
The prospect of Canada having to import a million barrels of oil a year has a very detrimental impact on the economic welfare of this nation. I would like to quote Jack Gallagher, the president of Dome Petroleum, when he spoke to the Canadian Institute of Strategic Studies last October. I have used these figures before, but I think they are important and they should be reiterated because they demonstrate and, indeed, highlight the impact of depending to any extent upon foreign oil to meet our domestic demands. He stated:
The economic impact of importing one million barrels per day of foreign oil at $15 per barrel has a negative effect on the economy of $5.5 billion per year. In contrast, using one million barrels per day of domestically produced oil at the same cost delivered in Toronto creates a positive annual economic benefit of $15.6 billion which includes payments to the various levels of government of $6.2 billion... In addition to the economic benefit of $15.6 billion from domestic oil. .. (Canada would realize) a saving in foreign exchange of $5.2 billion per year.
From a national economic point of view as well as in the area of security of supply, and our attempts to achieve the degree of self sufficiency we want in this country, it is important that these resources be developed.
It is worth mentioning that, according to the National Energy Board statistics, by 1985 we could be importing 52 per cent of our oil. If we take a figure of $20 per barrel that would work out to $8.5 billion per year, a huge drain that would be devastating to our balance of payments.
It has been suggested that if we proceed to establish a heavy oil upgrading facility, one that would produce 100,000 barrels of oil per day, our imports could be reduced by $730 million per year. The economic benefits to governments should be considered.
In the package put together by Pacific Petroleums Ltd., the company that is spearheading the heavy oil upgrading facility in Alberta, it is indicated that over a 20-year period taxes and royalties accruing to the federal government would amount to $2 billion, and to the provincial government, $2.6 billion. If the facility is not developed the oil will stay in the ground or be used to pave roads and parking lots and as a component in the manufacturing of building materials.

As one who resides in and represents the constituency where the city of Lloydminster is located, I think it is important to note the impact that this resource has and will have on the area. The Lloydminster type heavy crude oil pool affects in an economic way an area approximately 100 miles in radius. It has been estimated that some 75,000 people are affected by this industry, directly or indirectly.
It should be noted too that the heavy oil industry is very labour intensive, much more so than the conventional type of oil industry. It has been stated that approximately 34 per cent of the direct and secondary employment in Lloydminster is related to the heavy crude industry. It has been estimated that it takes the labour of one man for each producing well. Currently, in the immediate area, there are more than 3,000 producing wells which, using that formula, directly account for some 3,000 jobs.
Construction of a heavy oil upgrading plant costing $500 million to $700 million, and producing in the range of 100,000 barrels per day, would involve the employment of some 1,500 people. It is estimated that after completion 150 to 200 permanent staff would be required to operate it. There are, of course, the spin-off advantages of the development of the resource that would add to the already significant number of jobs created by the facility.
It has been pointed out by the members who have spoken earlier that current estimates suggest there are 16 billion barrels of heavy oil in the Lloydminster district. Using existing methods of extraction and even those methods in the process of being established, it is considered that only 5 to 10 per cent of the oil can be recovered. Methods being developed are so promising that it is hoped that it will be feasible to recover as much as 25 per cent to 30 per cent of the resource.
I think it is important that we get on with the job of building one upgrading facility at least in order to stimulate research into technology and the expertise that will be required if we are to recover a greater percentage of the available reserves.
I think it is wise to recap some of the history when we analyse the development of this important industry, Mr. Speaker. Heavy oil has been around for a long time. Husky Oil Ltd. has been involved in the Lloydminster area for many years. It is not something that has just been discovered, although I think the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) may just have found out about it recently.
In the days of cheap oil, there was no call on the resource. It was used to make asphalt for paving roads and for making other related items. The price increase by the OPEC cartel in 1973 changed this. Before the thought of establishing a heavy oil upgrading facility became popular, the industry was put in very serious jeopardy in 1974-75 through the export tax and the establishment of export quotas which affected this oil reserve as well as conventional reserves and put the heavy oil industry in a very serious position.
The bulk of this resource was exported to the United States because we did not have the capability in this country of upgrading it in our conventional refineries. Because of export
June 20, 1978

cutbacks and the export tax, that marketing opportunity was lost. When the markets dried up in the winter of 1975-76, hundreds of wells were closed. This had a very serious impact upon the industry because it costs so much to start up production again after closure, and some wells never regained their productive potential. This was a very serious set-back.
We brought this matter to the attention of the minister of this House. The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) and I made representations to the minister, and I must commend him for his response to them. He visited the area and Lloydminster, and saw first hand the impact that government policies were having upon this very important industry. As a result he set out to make some changes in the regulations, which in effect caused Husky Oil Ltd. and the other companies involved in the extraction of the resource to get back into the business.
At that time the minister realized the importance the heavy oil industry would have upon our over-all efforts to achieve self-reliance or self-sufficiency. I think the experience he gained there was part and parcel of the government's over-all policy to bring about the further development of this resource.
I should also say that Husky was at that time embarking upon an expansion program, a program to bring in a new refining facility, it was not as elaborate as the one talked about in recent days. However, they were initiating action on their own; it was not at the cajoling of the government or Petro-Canada.
When the minister expressed government policy, that it would encourage the further development of this resource and come up with some government programs and incentives to make it attractive, they immediately became interested in the establishment of an upgrading facility. They set out immediately to engage in discussions, consultations and negotiations with both the federal government and the provincial government of Saskatchewan, and later with Petro-Canada.
What looked like a very promising situation back in 1977 has been clouded by the foot-dragging of this minister, his inability to get the province of Saskatchewan and other interested parties together to provide the kind of leadership to back up this statement of producing a million barrels of synthetic oil a day by the year 1985 or 1990.
Having given that background, we now have to look at the best route and best method to develop this resource. We must ensure that the heavy oil which is extracted can be brought up to a specification suitable for our existing conventional refineries.
To be absolutely frank and honest, whether this resource is developed by the private sector or by a Crown corporation, it will only happen if we have a favourable climate in terms of a federal tax policy and in terms of what the provincial government and its royalty and tax structure will bring. We must bear in mind that we have to call upon the company that has proven expertise and experience and is prepared and willing to put its head on the line, so to speak, to develop this resource.
Natural Resources
In my view, Husky have pioneered the heavy oil industry. They are well prepared and have indicated a willingness to work with Occidental. Occidental expressed a willingness and, I am sure, are prepared to meet the deadlines and challenges in the development of this resource.
I urge the minister to forget his pet project, Petro-Canada, and to get on with the job of developing this resource. We need this resource. It can be used to the best advantage of all Canadians. It can be a very important element in our over-all objective of achieving that degree of self-sufficiency which we need in this country. Let Petro-Canada go into the boondocks to find some extra oil. As the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) stated, they have yet to prove that they are able to discover one barrel of oil.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I presumed it was his native province. He returned to Ottawa as a leader of a newly labelled party and continued in that position for ten years. He spent another seven illustrious years in what I consider to be, with a little bit of bias, a most important role in this House, and that is simply a member of parliament.
I wish to deal with the second part of the hon. member's motion, which reads:
-in order to avoid further domination and ownership of Canada's oil resources by foreign multi-national oil companies, and a continuing financial rip-off of the Canadian consumer, the development of Husky Oil Company's heavy oil resources should be undertaken by Petro-Canada in co-operation with the provinces directly affected.
We are looking at this Husky-Petro-Canada-Occidental issue of redevelopment of heavy oil when the total proven reserves of conventional oil in Canada stand at somewhere between six billion and seven billion barrels. As I understand it, that is enough to meet total Canadian needs for ten years at our present rate of consumption. That is really not very much oil.
This situation has received very critical and close attention by this government since the double whammy in 1973 when we experienced a quadrupling of world prices. There was an acknowledgement by our National Energy Board that our proven reserves were far less than what most Canadians had assumed prior to that time. Suddenly Canadians were faced

June 20, 1978
Natural Resources
with the fact that we were no longer a country with boundless reserves of oil and gas. That is the first point that has to be made, and it is an important one.
The next point is that there are still some Canadians who are understandably confused about this over-all picture. They do not really believe that there is a worldwide crisis developing in the near to immediate future in this area.
It is important to put a few figures on the record. My understanding of the world picture is that at the present time there are 646 billion barrels in place. That is being used up at the rate of 22 billion barrels a year. At most, this gives us about a 30 year supply at current consumption. That does not allow for any expansion in future.
By the turn of the century it is clear that we will have a worldwide problem on our hands. There is no point in our looking to the United States for potential support. Even at this time that country is importing 45 per cent of its needs.
What are we to do to counteract the problem? What have we done and what are we doing? First, we are moving to eliminate completely our exports of conventional crude to the United States. We are quickly moving to a point in the future where there will be no further exports. At the same time, this government has shown considerable leadership across the country in conservation measures. Canadians are subscribing to those measures more and more. They are doing everything they can both individually and collectively to keep down the further increasing demand which has been a normal factor in this country up to this time. On the one hand we are closing down exports, and on the other we are reducing demand. Both these actions have the combined effect of making a significant dent in the over-all demand for oil that ultimately becomes available to Canadians.
The next step I suggest is to look beyond the normal conventional sources to some of the more remote sources of potential oil supply. I think of the tar sands, the Beaufort Sea, the high Arctic and, of course, the heavy oils in the Lloydmin-ster area. In the meantime, until such resources are proven we must get along as net importers to the tune of some 250,000 barrels a day. We will probably continue in a net import position for many years into the future. The question we face is how to keep imports to the minimum.
What are we talking about when we refer to heavy oils? As a layman in this subject, I understand we are talking of a very thick, tacky substance which differs as much in texture from conventional western crude as day differs from night. We are speaking of a resource which, in order to be used in a conventional way, as we wish to use it, has to undergo an incredibly expensive upgrading process after extraction from the ground, the achievement of which is in itself extremely complicated and fantastically expensive. In essence, we are dealing with a quality of oil which modern scientific development enables to be extracted and ultimately used at a price which is far out of line with any cost we have heretofore

experienced in obtaining like quantities of oil from conventional sources.
The potential quantity of this oil is, indeed, impressive, so impressive that we cannot afford to ignore it in the face of the situation in which Canadians find themselves. I mentioned earlier that conventional reserves stand at between six and seven billion barrels. Heavy oils are conservatively estimated to contain 16 billion barrels and possibly as much as 20 or 25 billion barrels if we go all the way to tertiary recovery methods. At present we foresee ultimate production of anywhere up to 100,000 or 200,000 barrels per day from these various production methods. The figures I have used may be a little on the high side and be realized only in the distant future, but that is the potential.
Stated another way, the rate of production of heavy oils could ultimately cover up to 50 per cent of our current rate of imports. We are today producing in Canada some 1.4 million barrels of oil per day. Steadily decreasing resources of conventional supplies will reduce this figure to 400,000 barrels a day by 1995. By that time our over-all needs are estimated to reach two million barrels per day. Thus one can see a clear shortfall of 1.6 million barrels a day or, stated another way, we shall only be producing from conventional sources some 20 per cent at most of our over-all needs.
Therefore, unless in the next 15 years we can proceed with developments such as the tar sands, heavy oils, as well as continuing our exploration in the Beaufort Sea and the high Arctic, we shall be in a very vulnerable position at a time when world oil supplies will be shrinking in a very drastic way. There is certainly no guarantee that the problem will have been resolved by the discovery of great globs of oil from offshore.
Alternative resources are not only in themselves extremely expensive but will require dramatic lead-in periods of anywhere up to 30 or 40 years before they can be called upon to make a significant improvement in the over-all energy supply picture. What I am really saying, then, is that Canadians and the government which has duly been elected by them must show leadership in these nonconventional oil resource areas. We shall be facing very significant problems indeed if we fail to do so.
It is estimated that by 1995 some 800,000 to one million barrels per day of the then anticipated shortfall of 1.6 million barrels could be met from these new sources. In other words, if we get on with the job we could be curing some 50 per cent of the shortfall which will exist some 15 years hence. This is without giving any credit to potential discoveries in the Beaufort Sea or in the high Arctic. The reason no figures are projected in these areas is because the potential is still looked upon as simply that, and we do not have any significant proven figures available at this point.
As I have already said, we have to take action soon. The question is: how should we proceed? It is important that we waste no time in developing our heavy oil deposits. What mechanism should be utilized for this purpose? The technology is there. The heavy oil is there. How should this important new
June 20, 1978

Canadian oil resource be developed and by whom? Do we really care, Mr. Speaker? These questions have to be answered.
Allow me at the outset to state my bias in this regard. I consider myself to be as good a Canadian as any other member in this House. I believe in the strength of our country now, in its strength in the future, in its ability eventually to resolve issues relating to differing regional viewpoints across our vast land mass, in our ability to resolve difficulties arising from the adoption at the national level of two official languages, and in our ability to absorb and appreciate the benefits of a multicultural make-up.
I am sure 1 share with other members of this House pride at being a Canadian. I am proud of my country. But this does not mean that all developments in this country must be wrapped in Canadian ownership. Had this view been adopted in 1867, we would today in all likelihood be without a transcontinental railway, perhaps even an oil and gas industry. We are a trading nation and we must never forget it. Even Venezuela, from which we get a great deal of our imported oil, is an important buyer of Canadian goods at present. The Venezuelans want to continue to trade with Canadians in the years ahead and surely will do so. It is not necessary, in order to have social value, that everything must be Canadian.
What about the following situation-a situation where already over 80 per cent of our industry is controlled by persons outside Canada, by non-Canadians? Suppose that, in addition, we are facing a crisis of grave proportions. Husky Oil Limited has, I think, proved itself to be a good corporate citizen from the time of its inception some 40 years ago when it had 19 employees. What do we do, given these other parameters I have mentioned, when the Canadian corporation or its U.S. parent wants out? Should we be hiding our heads in the sand? Should we be saying: "Oh well, important resource or not, this company wants out; it is owned by non-Canadian interests so why not let non-Canadian interests replace it as new owners? Who cares about the 80 per cent non-Canadian ownership of the industry? After all, it has been there for years, so why bother?"
Well, Mr. Speaker, I believe the people of Canada do care and have cared for some time. The difficulty, as always, is how best to overcome an ownership imbalance of the present extent. My conclusion is this: an opportunity has been provided in the present instance and, in my view, it should be pursued-not at all costs but in a reasonable and rational way that is capable of being supported by the vast majority of Canadians.
This, 1 suggest, is what indeed is happening. The government-not with much encouragement or help from the official opposition, 1 must say-has created a Crown corporation to be an arm of the people in this great industry at a critical period. We were one of the last industrial nations to do so. This Crown corporation has, most properly in my view, made a bid to take over the Husky Oil Company. The company virtually controls most of the acreage in the Lloydminster area where the heavy oil play is taking place. People in my constituency and Canadi-
Natural Resources
ans at large would not want to see Petro-Can buy out Husky at an unreasonable price, unsupportable by the assets and potential on hand. However, I suggest most Canadians would indeed like to see Petro-Can actively involved in the takeover battle- as it seems to be developing-and not prepared to bow out at the first yelp from a giant non-Canadian counterbidder. That is what is taking place.
Personally, I hope Petro-Canada wins fairly and at a price supportable by the facts at hand. Alternatively, should the other bidder win-a non-Canadian corporation-it is my firm request to this government that before ever approving such a takeover it ensure through the mechanisms available to it and with approval from this parliament that beyond a shadow of a doubt the real interests of, and benefits to, Canadians are proved, perhaps in the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works of this House. This should be the assurance prior to any such approval being given.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to participate in this debate on the development of heavy oil reserves. I happen to share with my friend, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), representation of the city of the Lloydminster, Alberta-Saskat-chewan, which is the centre, geographically at least, of the Lloydminster heavy oil fields, as they have become known.
The hon. member for Vegreville spoke earlier this afternoon in this debate. He stressed, among other things, the importance of heavy oil development to that city and to that region of Alberta and Saskatchewan which will be directly affected. In that respect, as is indeed quite often the case, I share that concern with my hon. friend. We should welcome that economic development not only for what it will do in the way of reserves of oil for the nation as a whole but also for the people and businesses in our constituencies who will be involved directly and will benefit from this development.
Today's opposition motion involves a resource which has become a great deal more newsworthy and of much more concern to all Canadians, particularly those of us who represent areas where there are oil resources. The heavy oil reserves of Canada are centred around the Lloydminster area, as has been pointed out by other speakers. I am happy to say that the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the federal government, despite their different interests, responsibilities and roles, have been involved in encouraging the development of these reserves as well as the exploration which is so important to learning more about this great resource.
Various figures and statistics have been put on the record here this afternoon to indicate the scope of these reserves, and it is interesting to note how in recent years the scope and importance of those reserves have changed almost from year to year. I have here a clipping from the Edmonton Journal dated October 16, 1976. The headline reads: "Husky Oil sets Lloydminster heavy oil at 12 billion barrels". Part of the article reads as follows:

June 20, 1978
Natural Resources
Husky Oil Ltd. says the Lloydminster heavy oil deposit... contains 12 billion barrels of oil or three times the amount given in earlier estimates.
I think that is noteworthy. The article goes on to discuss additional reserves and says the following:
Additional reserves can undoubtedly be found in other sands... Husky has interests in 1.6 million acres of the three million acre area involved in the study.
Mr. Nielson-
Mr. Nielson is the president of Husky Oil.
-said it is difficult to estimate how much of the 12 billion barrels of oil in place can be recovered because of difficulties involved in producing heavy oil.
This question was discussed by my friend, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) who just resumed his seat. The article goes on:
The company has operated for 30 years in the Lloydminster area and has achieved 4 per cent recovery of the oil in place by conventional or primary production methods.
1 think the last statement relative to the very low rate of recovery is another important aspect of this whole debate on heavy oil, whether that recovery is accomplished by Husky or any other company, privately owned, Crown owned or whatever. We need two things. We need upgrader facilities, but above all we need better and improved technology to get a greater and better recovery rate. Those two factors are very much involved in any discussion of heavy oil development.
I think it was the hon. member for Vegreville who mentioned earlier that the heavy crude reserves in the Lloydminster area were associated, up until the last four, five or six years, primarily with the construction industry. They were associated with the asphalt industry, whether for highways, parking lots or shingles. As a result it was largely a seasonal operation and production was geared to market demands which were pretty well localized. If we check the figures for production by Husky and other producers of heavy oil in the Lloydminster area over the years, we find that production gradually climbed to accommodate that market until 1973 when the importance of any reserve of oil became much more pronounced. The picture had changed dramatically. I suppose it also changed with the development of sour crude or heavy crude refineries to handle that kind of crude oil. Incidentally, these refineries were not located in Canada and still are not located in Canada. They have been in existence to date only in the United States of America.
That is some of the background which forms the basis for the current importance we place on these reserves and on our search to become more energy self-sufficient. As we look down the road and as we listen to the figures in this debate it becomes obvious to anyone that it is important that this country get on with developing the heavy oil reserves located in the Alberta-Saskatchewan border area.
The politics of oil in recent years have certainly been well known to all of us. I suggest that has been in a direct way because of the dramatic price increases with which we as individuals and industries have been faced in this country and in others which have been directly affected by the dramatic increase following the formation of the OPEC cartel. Mr. Speaker, I see that you are ready to call it six o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before we adjourned for supper at six o'clock I spent a moment or two emphasizing the importance, not only to all of Canada but to my part of Saskatchewan and that part of the province represented by my hon. friend who participated in the debate this afternoon, the hon. member for Vegreville, of the development of heavy oil. 1 commented on the size of the reserves and on other factors affecting their development. In that respect, a pamphlet referred to by the minister in his remarks earlier this afternoon entitled "Oil Sands and Heavy Oils: The Prospects", contains a paragraph on page 14 which, I think, sums up very well the whole picture of the heavy oil reserves in the Lloydminster area. It reads:
The range of estimates of recoverable oil could therefore give rise to ultimate total production from Lloydminster-type heavy-oil tertiary recovery projects ranging from 100,000 barrels per day to as much as 300,000 barrels per day or more. As mentioned, such development may take a decade or longer to achieve-
So we are not speaking about something that is likely to happen tomorrow or next week. It reads that that development-
-will depend heavily upon the continued successful development and application of tertiary recovery methods and will require the establishment of an economic environment receptive to enhanced recovery projects... an essential part of such an environment.
That, more or less, sums up the potential and the possibilities for Canada of that reserve.
Going back to the time of the OPEC crisis which brought all of us in Canada to take a second look, and indeed more than a second look, at the energy picture in this country, I think it was about that time when those of us not directly involved in the oil industry suddenly came to realize that we in Canada were not floating on a sea of oil, a conviction which was generally and widely held by Canadians. I am not sure it is fair to say this but perhaps this was encouraged by governments and by the oil companies themselves. That conviction was certainly shattered for us as we became more aware of the real facts and figures with respect to our oil reserves.
I say "real facts" with full knowledge that real facts are somewhat difficult to come by and to translate in that sense. It is one thing to speak about potential reserves, recoverable reserves, proven reserves, and so on, and these terms in themselves were not that familiar, I am sure, to many of us. Perhaps they lulled us into believing that we thought we had ample reserves here in the country, that we did not need to import oil, and therefore we were sitting pretty, happy with a good and cheap source of oil. But we suddenly realized at
June 20, 1978

about that time that we were not self-sufficient as a nation. We also came to realize that some of the great reserves we have here in Canada are still unproven, particularly in the case of the northern and the Arctic reserves, and that they are very costly to develop, and we have had Syncrude and the tar sands efforts to prove it. In this motion we are discussing the possibility and the potentiality of heavy oil development.
Again at that time we had it brought home to us that these energy reserves were almost entirely foreign owned by the same companies which were active in the Middle East and the North Sea and other areas around the world. As has been pointed out in the debate this afternoon, governments are in the oil business in almost every oil-producing country, and they are in it today more so than ever before.
To listen this afternoon to some of my friends from the Conservative party taking part in the debate one would think that Canada had the monopoly on a new or innovative idea or project to legislate into existence a Crown-owned resource company now known as Petro-Canada. In this particular case we were not leading the pack. Instead, as a nation we are trailing the pack in so far as the oil-producing countries of the world are concerned.
The concept of Petro-Canada is not new. Certainly it has my support. I do not share the concern of some hon. members opposite that this agency must be in conflict with the private sector in oil. The private sector must be maintained and encouraged. There is ample room for both. At this time Canada requires both the publicly owned Petro-Canada on the one hand and the private sector on the other. Much of the conflict is in the minds of some members opposite.
In 1973, 1974 and 1975 the Canadian oil industry faced some adjustments which were unique to Canada because of its federal nature. The oil industry spokesmen were quite vocal in their criticism, much of which was justified.
As a result of the dramatic rise in the world price, a see-saw developed between the federal and provincial governments over the windfall margins. One can sympathize with the oil companies which operated during the period when governments at both levels re-examined their interests in oil development, whether it be in the form of royalties, income taxes or other regulations pertaining to oil policies. One's sympathies must be tempered to some degree by the healthy balance sheets which continued to appear in the year-end reports of oil companies. The oil companies came out of that tug-of-war fairly well. Exploration activities in Alberta and Saskatchewan have increased dramatically. The results have been good. Over the last number of months the stock market has been good evidence of that recovery as well.
The motion before the House is in two parts. The first part asks for new resource developments in Canada to be majority Canadian controlled. I am sure that principle is supported by all parties in this House.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!
Natural Resources

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
1 have enough respect for Canadian oil companies to believe that they can do the job. We have no guarantee that development will occur otherwise. It will occur only, outside of Canadian ownership and involvement, if such development in Canada fits within the over-all, worldwide scheme of things. I am sure the plans of large oil companies are changed quite often on the basis of good businesslike decisions, rather than anything the government or the country does. That does not serve the interests of Canada in becoming self-sufficient, nor does it keep our priorities in order.
Some members of the Conservative party indicated that Petro-Can should not develop Canadian heavy oil. Others in the past have indicated that they would scrap and abolish that company. The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) implied that Husky, which has a very large stake in Canadian heavy oil, has been prevented by the government from developing those great stocks and reserves. Husky has not done badly by the federal government or the two provinces involved. The management of Husky Oil has not made such charges against the government. Husky has been in Saskatchewan and Alberta for many years. It has had discussions with Petro-Can and others over recent months regarding the possibility of sale or partnerships. It is not necessary to recount the recent offers and activities in that sense; the papers have performed an adequate job in that regard. The business section of today's Globe and Mail carried several articles containing a good deal of background elaboration on these proposals.
Hon. members of the Conservative party asked how much oil Petro-Can has discovered. The question is a good one but it is not relevant to this debate. In so far as heavy oil is concerned, it is not a question of discovery; it is a question of recovery.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Heavy oil reserves exist. It is a question of getting a greater percentage of those reserves to the surface. It has been estimated that approximately 16 billion barrels of oil are under the 1.6 million acres which Husky Oil controls. Primary recovery of heavy oil is very low; it is 4 per cent to 6 per cent, and perhaps up to 10 per cent. Improved recovery technology is an important factor in this debate. It must proceed and go hand in hand with building an upgrader.
For Canadians to utilize the energy reserves of heavy oil, two things must happen. We need an upgrader plant or facility to handle the heavy oil, and we need improved technology for tertiary recovery of the raw resource so that we can feed oil stock into it. The federal government and the provincial government of Saskatchewan signed a $16 million agreement to stimulate research in this area. As I understand it, Husky Oil submitted an application which was later withdrawn for

June 20, 1978
Natural Resources
unknown reasons. Other small oil companies in the area have initiated programs to move in this direction.
The federal government must do all it can to ensure that heavy oil development takes place as soon as possible in the interests of this country. As a beginning step, the government can deal very quickly with the purchase bid by Occidental. FIRA should be able to determine, without any great lengthy study, that Occidental may have a pretty hefty cheque book but has no expertise in the heavy oil development field. Husky Oil has such expertise. According to telephone calls which I received, Petro-Can has some expertise and is acquiring more. So that expertise is available in the country.
The second part of the hon. member's motion indicates that Petro-Canada should develop Husky Oil's heavy oil reserves together with Alberta and Saskatchewan. In principle I support that, if Husky Oil does not show more determination to put forth the required initiative and drive to bring about that development than it has. I have no objection to private Canadian oil interests being involved as partners. In fact, I welcome that. When the private sector cannot or does not, for whatever reason-and there may be good reason from their point of view-develop Canadian resources in accord with the expressed national interests of this country, the question is, what is our next step?
I suggest that Husky has, indeed, had ample time to make its intentions known. I agree Husky has been negotiating, but it is my view that the company has not been sufficiently forthright in telling any level of government what its firm intention is. That is my view as an observer; I am not thoroughly acquainted with the oil industry. I just suggest that we should not wait years or even months, but perhaps a few weeks, before asking Petro-Can to continue to get on with the job, hopefully in co-operation with the private sector and provincial governments.
In that regard I want to commend the minister for his interest and the efforts he has made to bring about heavy oil development. The minister announced a $16.4 million program a year or two ago. Every budget in the last three or four years has contained steps and measures devised to encourage and bring about oil exploration and development. The most recent budget that came down, the one we are continuing to debate in the House, contains special measures for the development of heavy oil reserves in western Canada. I welcome these changes, but would ask how much more we have to do before that development takes place, or how much longer we have to wait for Husky Oil to announce its intention to proceed with the development-because, indeed, Husky Oil is a key player in this particular field.
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and I thank my colleagues for allowing the additional time.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in the debate on the motion of my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The

Islands (Mr. Douglas). This motion relates to an issue that directly affects the province of Saskatchewan and the province of Alberta, as well as the entire country.
I listened this afternoon to my friends and colleagues in the Conservative caucus making statements to the effect that Petro-Can should be disbanded and that the whole development of heavy crude oil in the Lloydminster area of Saskatchewan and Alberta should be left in the hands of private Canadian investors and companies. The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) made reference to two Canadian consortiums which were prepared to make offers to Husky. I have a question that I hope some members in the official opposition will answer. Where the hell were those private Canadian investors and companies in the past when we needed them and where are they now that we need them again?
In fact, who are those two alleged Canadian consortiums? I am satisfied that a Liberal private enterprise government would not go to the length of having Petro-Can bid for Husky unless all other opportunities and sources had been exhausted. It would be the last, along with the official opposition, to get into some kind of public ownership in the petroleum industry. Surely it is obvious that the so-called Canadian entrepreneurs, private investors and companies in the petroleum industry have let us and Canada as a whole down.
The official opposition condemns Crown corporations because of the "incompetence" of Crown corporations. I notice members of that party go to great lengths in condemning Crown corporations that have usually been established and operated under the Liberals and Conservatives. The question is not so much one of whether the operation is private or public, but rather how well the operation is run and who are the people running it.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre complains about our tax laws. As a result of talking to relatives, friends and other people in the petroleum industry on the telephone in the last day or two, as well as over the years since 1947, I am convinced that since the Leduc discovery Canadian companies and Canadian investors, no matter what the ills associated with our tax laws, have done very well thank you. But that is not a sufficient excuse for an alleged Canadian consortium or company letting us down.
When it gets to the point where a private enterprise Liberal government is encouraging and assisting a Crown corporation such as Petro-Can in making bids for shares of the Husky Oil Company, this tells us something about the private sector in Canada, the petroleum industry. What is even more important is a consideration of the outfit that is bidding for Husky shares in competition with Petro-Can. I talked with a knowledgeable person today from the oil industry in Western Canada whose opinion of Occidental can be given as follows: It does not have a lot to offer; it is primarily a gas company; it does not have any particular skills in heavy crude production or refining and will rely on Husky for that expertise; and it has done no research and development in respect of upgrading or refining of heavy crude oil.
June 20, 1978

What is also interesting is that in the deal Occidental is offering Husky it is not putting up much, if any, money. It is offering a straight trade-off of shares. 1 am sure the management or board of directors of Occidental are not stupid. They are offering to buy Husky through a trade-off of shares with no expenditure of money. They are doing this because they think there are some bucks to be made out of it, and for no other reason. 1 do not want anybody in this House to suggest to me that Occidental is making this offer in competition with a Canadian Crown corporation because management of that company has some particular worry or fear about the welfare and good order of Canadian energy supplies or the development of Canadian crude oil.
I wish the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), or his government, had made it plain some two or three weeks ago that, no matter what Occidental bids, it will not be allowed in here. I wish the minister had said: "We neither need them nor want them, and certainly in view of what that company is offering, we certainly do not need them".
There are some 2.1 million acres in the heavy crude area of Lloydminster presently held by various companies. Husky Oil holds about 1.6 million acres, 70 per cent being on the Saskatchewan side of the border and 30 per cent on the Alberta side. A few other companies hold a small number of acres each, including Murphy Oil, Mobil Oil, Imperial Oil and Petro-Can. Petro-Can bought a few acres not long ago, and Saskoil holds a few acres as well. They do not count for much separately. Husky holds the major portion of the area.
At the present time about 50,000 barrels of heavy crude are being produced for which there is a market. The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) mentioned this. It is used for asphalt and asphalt shingles. It is actually an assured market. Even when Husky proposed late last year an upgrading and refining capacity of up to 100,000 barrels a day, during discussion with the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan and the federal authorities the idea all of a sudden dried up. Husky chickened out; cut and ran.
There is good reason for that. What is commonly not known is that Husky Oil does not have the needed cash flow. They do not have the muscle or the borrowing capacity to move in; otherwise they would not be considering offers from Petro-Canada, Occidental or anyone else. Husky Oil is not noted in the industry for research and development, expansion or further development of heavy crude production. They have simply been sitting on it. This may be good for the Nielson boys and the present shareholders of Husky, but I submit it is not very good for the people of Canada, or the self-sufficiency of this country which members on all sides of the House have been talking about.
From the Saskatchewan point of view, where most of this acreage is, the Husky holdings should remain in Canadian hands. From a developmental point of view, if it remains in
Natural Resources
Canadian hands the pace of development will be in the hands of the federal government and the two provinces concerned. If it is in American hands, however, how much incentive will those two provinces and the national government have to give them to get a good pace of development? The pace of production and development must be set at a rate which we think is best for Canada. If the ownership and control of that acreage and that production remains in American hands, we will have to pay more in order to get a pace of development in production which will suit our needs and our requirements.
For Canada to have that development, whether it is in production of heavy crude or the construction of pilot projects, and upgrading capacities of heavy crude, we must have the control to set a pace which we think is best for us and best to further Canadian self-sufficiency. Husky has refused to move. Of course, they were pioneers in the heavy crude business, and they were in it at the beginning. I gave them credit for that and for being smart in amassing a large acreage of land. But they do not have a large cash flow and they have had small growth because they have been more interested in truck stops and service stations than in research and development in the production of heavy crude. They have made no breakthrough in the area of development and their research has been minimal.

speechtext: Who has?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
None of the private sector has, Mr. Speaker. It is only now that a so-called free enterprise Liberal government has realized that the private sector, both Canadian and American, have let the country down. There have been no breakthroughs on development. There has been insufficient money from Husky to do it, and everybody in the oil industry, the two provincial governments and the national government darn well know that. The final criticism of Husky, while they were sitting on their fat acreage, is that they themselves have not developed much expertise in the upgrading of heavy crude oil. They have been sitting waiting for windfalls since 1973, and they landed one when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the government allowed their own creature, Petro-Canada, to be bounced back and forth between Husky and Occidental in a crap game which has increased the value of Husky shares far out of proportion to their real worth on the open market.
My hon. friend the member for Calgary Centre was talking before supper about the Canadian taxpayer paying for Petro-Canada. He failed to mention that Canadian consumers have paid for all the profits and the expenses, including operational and development costs. The Canadian consumers by buying heating oil or by buying gas at the pumps have paid the entire bill, so I do not want to hear any more nonsense about the private enterprise entrepreneur who took all the so-called risks. Any of them who lost money recovered it one way or another, whether it was through tax losses or profits made in some other operation. The Canadian consumer, not the Canadian taxpayer, whether or not they paid income taxes or corporation

June 20, 1978
Natural Resources
taxes, paid for and continue to pay for all the developmental costs.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has allowed a company owned by the people of Canada to be put into a position of having to fork over $200 million or $250 million because Occidental has got in the game. They would not know a barrel of heavy crude if it hit them in the face. This is not leadership, Mr. Speaker. This is not exercising sovereignty or nationhood. We neither earn nor deserve respect from other governments or, more particularly, from foreign-owned corporations that know they can play games with weak-kneed, lily-livered, nervous-Nelly governments. This government wants to be a little public and a little private, and they cannot make up their minds which one.
I can say for the Tories that at least you know where they stand, Mr. Speaker. As far as they are concerned, Occidental Oil is welcome to come up here; Occidental Oil can have a deal which would make you and I look brilliant, if we could have an operation like that. Occidental has proposed a scheme which says that the Saskatchewan and Alberta governments can put up $200 million or $300 million apiece on the one hand, and Petro-Canada can put up $400 million to $600 million. It works out to approximately one-third each, one-third for the two provinces, one-third for Petro-Canada and the other third for Occidental.
Let us look at what Occidental wants back for their investments. This, Mr. Speaker, is what you would call real private enterprise. Occidental would continue to retain all the rights for the primary and secondary production in heavy crude in the acreage which they have developed, which is only approximately 280,000 acres. They have about one million other acres yet to drill in. Occidental would also retain all the conventional rights. Occidental is not interested in keeping the rights of the highly expensive tertiary recovery system but they would retain everything else.
I do not know if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is high-handed or easily taken, but with a deal such as that it is no wonder Occidental is offering to trade shares with Husky at $2 or $3 a share more than what Petro-Canada is bidding. In fact, if the minister rose in his place, or preferably the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and made it known publicly that no matter what Occidental does they will not be approved to operate in this country, they would save the investors of Canada.

I hope this government will remember why they created Petro-Canada in the first place. Both Petro-Can and the cabinet have agreed that rapid development of the heavy oil deposits around Lloydminster is a national priority, yet they sit around and let an outfit like Occidental mess it up, a company that has no expertise in heavy oil and which is not putting up any money for Husky Oil Ltd.

(a) all major new resource developments should be majority Canadian controlled as promised by the government during the 1974 federal election campaign;
How can this be achieved? It is very simple. First of all, the federal government does not have the right to step into natural resource development, which belongs to the provinces. The NDP does not recognize this at all. For the New Democrats, whether socialism is federal or provincial does not matter. It is socialism anyway.

I have listened to these people on the political left talk about resources. It is just pitiful. Even before the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) was into short pants the Alberta oil industry was developing. He is a newcomer to this particular subject because of his age. When it came to the development of the oil industry in the province of Alberta, if we Canadians lost control of the freeholds it was because of our tax system. We have nobody to blame but ourselves. How are we to guarantee that Canadians will be in charge or have financial control of all new major developments of natural resources? Not through the doctrinaire remedy of public ownership. The proposer of today's motion is a former premier of the province of Saskatchewan.
