speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as usual, the opposition day dedicated to Petro-Canada, Husky Oil and the heavy oil deposits in Alberta and Saskatchewan focuses on a few features which I would like to name. First is the role of Petro-Canada in the Canadian energy picture and the socialistic imputations of the NDP demand for government takeovers. Second is the ability of FIRA to determine a foreign take-over bid in terms of being likely to help Canada, and third is the suggestion in the motion that we should make sure
June 20, 1978

50 per cent or 60 per cent of the capital in all the take-overs or branch plants here is Canadian. Finally, there is the whole question of a branch plant economy in Canada.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) gave an excellent speech today. He fears the eventual economic absorption of Canada by the United States of America. Like many of us on both sides of the House, he wants to see this country's natural resources completely under Canadian control. Everybody would like to see that if possible. But to underline, as he did, that the oil companies get 95 per cent of equity, sales and profits is to tell only half the story. Mr. Speaker, the provincial and federal governments get a great deal more out of a barrel of oil produced in Canada than do the oil companies.
This, of course, is due to taxes and royalties. After all, income tax is charged against Canadian-owned and United States-owned branch plants alike. Then, of course, the branch plant pays income tax again to its own government. There is an implied criticism of the government for not ensuring that the 50 per cent or 60 per cent investment clause is enforced. Mr. Speaker, investments made by Canadians are free to go anywhere. There is no mandatory requirement for investment to be made only in Canadian securities and companies. In fact, to recall all our foreign investment and to force all Canadian capital into Canadian enterprises could only be done by an authoritarian or Marxist government. What is more, it would limit and cramp the flow of capital and affect international interdependence and our foreign trade balance. In a short time we would be financially worse off.
As the minister said in his speech today, Canada has 14 principles for the guidance of foreign companies operating in Canada. Two of them require the companies to operate in Canada's interests, and to enable Canadians to buy into such companies because private capital was not in great enough supply to ensure sufficient Canadian representation. For that reason Petro-Canada was given certain exploration rights and opportunities to buy into firms where only a minimum amount of Canadian money had been subscribed.
Despite the charge by many nationalists that Canada is only a branch plant economy, we still do very well in our foreign trade balance. It was said recently by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in this House:
Canada has shown a positive trade balance for the last 17 consecutive months whereas in the U.S.A., which invests heavily in Canada, the foreign trade balance has been adverse for 32 months.
That is almost twice as long as Canada's favourable balance has lasted. So I suppose if we were a socialist state-and I hope to goodness we never are-we would take over or nationalize foreign companies in Canada just as is done in Venezuela or Saudi Arabia. Those are not socialistic states, of course; they are authoritarian. We could even demand that branch plants, after a period of time, be given the right by their foreign parent to compete for domestic, United States and foreign markets and, equally, initiate their own research and development. I believe that eventually this would be a good policy to adopt.
Natural Resources
I would very much 'ike to see all branch plants doing their own research and development eventually, but that would be Utopia. It is, though, a possible target to bear in mind. The fear that Occidental would not operate in Canada's best interests seems to me to be unfounded because the American capital and profits would have brought much revenue to provincial and federal governments.
The concept of Petro-Canada must be much better understood than it is. The corporation was created for more than one reason. At the time of its inception exploration for oil and gas, which is almost completely in private hands, had begun to wind down. Drilling rigs were moving to Venezuela, the Gulf of Mexico or to the North Sea. Canada was importing several hundred thousand barrels of oil daily at an almost quadrupled world price. The prospect of serious energy shortages in the 1980s emphasized the need for energetic exploration and development of our oil and gas resources on the prairies, in the Arctic and offshore on our eastern continental shelf. In other words, Canada needed to become self-reliant, if not self-sufficient, in energy. It goes without saying that our oil, gas and coal, which are present in large quantity, must all be developed before renewable energy resources come on stream because of the time lag in their technical application.
I would like to refer to a speech made by the Hon. Donald Macdonald on March 12, 1975. In that speech he said:
The best way to secure a Canadian presence, a rate of development consistent with our national interest, a proper share of the income generated by such activity and full access to new technology, is by a direct government involvement in key ventures through a corporation which can develop the necessary expertise. Our national petroleum company would then be in a position to act as a catalyst for succeeding projects, assisting in their planning and financing as well as participating ultimately in their revenues.
Part of our national energy policy is to keep costs to the consumer fairly equal from east to west and also to keep the Canadian price below the world price. It cannot be too far below or our income from taxes, royalties and duties will not allow the revenue from our own resources to ensure continued exploration and development in our costly Canadian geographical position.
The "rip-off' argument, which is that we are determined to raise Canadian oil prices on July 1 in spite of the freeze by OPEC, is not substantiated. Our Canadian crude oil price will still be $2.50 below the world price, even with the increase of $1 a barrel. We will still be well below Washington, London and Paris in our cost of heating oil. Even if the price of our gas is not lower than the U.S. price, it is about the same, and at least our supply will continue for a much longer time, while the future for American gas consumers is rather uncertain.
So it has been Petro-Canada's strategy to become interested in diverse fossil fuels. There are huge deposits of coal present in Nova Scotia, B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan and also in the Arctic, for instance, on Baffin Island. A major intention is to develop coal as a substitute for imported oil-many oil companies are diversifying like that-or as a supplement or to assist as a fuel in extracting more oil from both the heavy oil

June 20, 1978
Natural Resources
deposits and the tar sands themselves. Eventually coal will offer great potential for electricity generation. Many new technologies are becoming practical, and combinations of coal powder and oil may soon be in use. Eventually coal may be liquefied and produce methanol and low Btu gasification.
Right now Petro-Canada is taking a leading role in evaluating our northern oil and gas reserve potential. By far the largest proportion of the country's oil and gas resources is in the far north. This becomes one of the most important tasks now laid on the shoulders of this national oil company. By 1990, 45 billion 1975 dollars will have to be spent on exploration and development in our frontier region. The role of Petro-Canada is very important. It is easy for many of us on both sides of the House to understand this frontier exploration and its importance because the Standing Committee of National Resources and Public Works toured the tar sands, the Mackenzie Delta, the high Arctic and Alaska. It was a very memorable trip which contributed greatly to our understanding. There is now increased interest on the part of the Canadian people in our frontier resources.
Recently Petro-Canada became interested in coal as well as oil and gas because of significant discoveries. There is now the promise of significant fossil fuels offshore in the Greenland-Labrador-Newfoundland triangle as well as on the Grand Banks, the Scotia Shelf and in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Without the leadership and intense effort exhibited by Petro-Canada, these resources might lie dormant and unexplored for many years.
This agency is not entirely profit-motivated. Although it is happy to increase its earned income, it is principally a government corporation bent on finding fuel reserves of many kinds which will insulate us from future early disappearance of our national energy self-reliance, and it will provide catalytic action in technology for refining and supply.
Finally, we on the government side are intensely interested in the orderly development of our fossil fuel reserves. We intend to use Petro-Canada to fulfil its function in petroleum supply, in exploration of our frontiers and in development of the very unique technology required so that we can use our gas, oil and coal properly. These fuels are in abundant supply. All that is needed is leadership. This, I can truly say, is being provided by this government and its energy agent, Petro-Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard many statements tonight, including statements from hon. members to my left, and one of the things about the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) which struck me, was his statement that Canada has done many great things in the past. There is no doubt that Canadians have done much in the past of which they can be proud, but I think it goes almost without question that the things which have been done by Canadians in the past have been done by the private sector. They have been done by free enterprise. It was the private sector which built this country.
[Mr. Railton.l
I do not think any of us can point with pride to anything which the Government of Canada has been involved in, created or is presently involved in. We only have to look at Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. What a sorry example! If the government would concentrate on delivering the mail, it probably would be taxing its abilities, and that has been proved.
We are discussing the question of foreign ownership of petroleum reserves in Canada. Surely it is better to have reserves in Canada which are foreign owned, if necessary, than to import foreign owned crude from other lands where supply is not secure. Surely it would be better to have crude oil produced by Occidental Petroleum, Exxon, or any other company, for that matter, coming from Alberta wells than crude oil coming from those same companies in Libya or the Middle East. Heavy capital needs are a fact of life in the petroleum industry, and in my view it is immaterial who owns the reserves. The vital question is not whether a company is French, Canadian or American. The vital question is whether we have supplies of oil for Canada's future. Because I do not think for one minute that even a member of the NDP would turn down a barrel of oil, if that is what is required to heat his home, or a cubic foot of gas just because it carried the label of an American company. When it gets right down to supply, even members of the NDP would be just as anxious to have a foreign label as a Canadian label. I do not give a damn, and I do not think Canadians should, about who owns the oil. I think the crux of the matter is whether we have it.
In spite of that, I do not think there is any question, and Canadians have always said they want to own as much of their own oil as they can. That was well stated by my hon. colleague who spoke last. However, the tax laws of Canada have prevented Canadians from owning this important resource. Only recently and at the urging of this party did the government finally cave in and make rules to encourage Canadian capital. That was a little late, and that is the reason we now face the fact that a large percentage of our crude oil is owned by foreign companies.
We also heard from the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that we have only a ten-year supply. If the matter of future supply is so critical, it seems to me that if Canadians were given incentives and had the good sense to go out and explore for oil, they could provide supplies for beyond 10 or 15 years at a time when present supplies are dwindling seriously.
Another statement made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was that Canada's oil reserves are not in the control of Canadians. There is no other industry in Canada that is more controlled than the oil and gas industry. The producing rate is controlled by the provincial governments; the price is controlled by the federal government; there is presently an export tax-the federal government takes the difference between the world price and the fixed Canadian price; the royalties are set and collected by provincial governments; income tax, through depletion allowances and tax rates,
June 20, 1978

is collected by the federal government. Also transportation tariffs are set by the federal government; pipeline construction routes and approvals are dictated by the federal government; companies under the new petroleum monitoring act, which this minister is trying to have passed, will have to report to the government on what they did with their income and they will have to prove that it was spent on finding new reserves; the sales tax on gasoline is payable to the federal government and to the provincial governments on gasoline that is sold, and this amounts to something in the order of $5 a barrel; and finally, it is the right of this government to determine through the Foreign Investment Review Board whether the reserves or shares of a company may be sold to those outside of Canada. So there is no question that Canada controls its oil and gas. It always has and there is no reason to think this is going to change.
When it comes to the rewards for oil and gas that is produced-and this was stated in a report put out by the Canada West Foundation Study-taxes and payments to all levels of government now represent approximately 70 per cent of the mineral resource industry's pretax profits, compared to 53 per cent five years ago. Any oil man with good sense who owns all the land and has all the royalty rights would much prefer to farm out his land to someone who would put up the risk dollars and give to that owner 30 per cent. 1 can tell the House that that is a very good deal for investors, and it is on the basis of the government not putting up risk moneys but just sitting back and collecting what is its due under our terms. Incidentally, this is comparable with or perhaps better for Canada than the situation in most countries where foreign oil companies go to search for oil and gas.
Let us look at the specifics of the motion, which states that the development of Husky Oil Company's heavy oil resources should be undertaken by Petro-Canada in co-operation with the provinces directly affected. In the past-and I guess it will be the same in the future-when socialists have seen something big which worked, they wanted to nationalize it. I have heard a lot said about Husky Oil tonight. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) made many serious allegations about a company which would be regarded by most as a good company and a good corporate Canadian citizen. When I arrived in the city of Edmonton from the Peace River country in 1952, Husky was one of the big names in heavy oil development at that time. They were drilling wells, they were building rigs, they were getting their refinery going, and that was 25 years ago. Since then others have come into the picture, but this company has pioneered in heavy oil development. They just happened to have the foresight or the luck to be today in the right place at the right time.
The minister is blaming energy shortfalls on all kinds of things, but the fact of the matter is that it is his responsibility. This government has done more to inhibit oil and gas exploration in recent years than any other factor in the realities of the Canadian oil and gas industry. More momentum has been lost and more rigs have been moved out.
Natural Resources
The setbacks caused by the two or three years of confrontation which was provoked by this government have been a big factor in lost reserves. The momentum has now returned, but I can tell hon. members that the losses experienced in those three or four years will never be regained. The Husky poker game is just another factor that has caused loss of confidence among investors in the Canadian oil and gas industry. Maybe it is the government's policy not to want Americans to invest in our oil and gas industry. Or that may be the policy of the NDP. But if Canadians do not have enough capital or resources to develop our reserves, I say we should invite foreign capital to assist and participate in this with us.
However, the government is trying to solve through its instrument, Petro-Canada, a problem that it has created itself. The government seems to go around creating problems so it will have something to solve. If we look at the problem which faces the Husky Oil Company, we find that it is a pretty serious one. The government is concerned because Husky Oil is not moving fast enough; but in every business plan and in every equation you must have all the squares and all the lines filled in, and there is a big X in the equation of anyone who wants to build an oil plant and extract heavy oil or, as in the case of Husky, build an upgrading plant.
This big X results from a number of considerations. The first is uncertainty of market. There is no guarantee of market. This is something for which these companies have been asking for some time. There is no certainty of price. These companies have sought the world price because everything is founded on that price so the capital investment can be made and the return on the investment realized. There is no royalty regime in the provinces of Saskatchewan or Alberta. How could anybody build a plant and plan to produce oil at very great cost and with heavy capital investment if they do not even know what the royalty will be? Presumably the federal initiatives in one of the Turner budgets which made royalties paid to the provinces non-deductible as an expense-in other words, companies paid tax on something they did not get-is still a matter that has never been resolved. When it comes down to financing a plant, it is not simply a question of whether the company wants to puts its money into the project but rather whether the bankers want to put their money into it. This is not dictated simply by oil company executives or by boards of directors, but by bankers. Nevertheless, governments are the problem-no royalties, no rules, no price.
I suggest that no other company could have put this together. Husky Oil Company is probably the most prominent in making frequent visits to this city and in dialoguing with members of the House in its attempts to keep us abreast of what is going on and what their problems are. I suggest, quite differently from my colleagues in the NDP, that Husky has been a good citizen, and I am very surprised to hear the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre say that they are too small a company to carry out this project. Certainly it is a big project and I suppose that what the NDP expects is bigness; but I think it is important in our country that small Canadian

June 20, 1978
Natural Resources
companies carry out and finance these projects. We are not all for bigness. Our small companies must also be able to do this.
Now we come right down to the question of solutions. I say that it is the minister who has failed to give us the solutions, and it is the minister who should have brought the parties to the table to sort these problems out. He should have brought the companies, the provinces, the federal government and, if necessary, Petro-Canada to the table to solve this problem, not have a confrontation.
A purchase by Petro-Canada achieves nothing except the fact that some $300 million to $500 million will go out of Canada at a time when our exchange rate is low. When the former minister of energy, mines and resources introduced his bill, he said, as reported in Hansard for March 12, 1975:
This bill is a most important element in the government's long term planning to secure adequate supplies of energy to meet our national needs. It is firmly rooted in the basic objectives of our energy and resource policies which are, to ensure for Canadians adequate and reliable supplies at reasonable prices-
Most people knowledgeable in the industry say that the way to achieve reasonable prices is to have some experts, some keen minds, figuring out where to drill and how to get this oil out of the ground, not to buy oil. Purchasing oil from others results in high cost oil. Those who took the risk and found oil obviously want more money. This does not seem to be included in what Petro-Can was originally asked to do. However, the emphasis by the minister and the government at that time was on future supply of oil and gas. This transaction, which involves a very large amount of money, does not find or produce for Canadians one single barrel of oil.
Perhaps an additional offer will be made by a Canadian company for the shares of Husky. We will have to wait and see. In the meantime, I propose that the government should urge the partnership of Occidental and Husky to come before the Foreign Investment Review Board so they can put forward their proposal. We must see what it is. Presently it is cited as a plan of significant benefit to Canada. If it is of significant benefit to Canada, and if their proposal contains any realism, surely their plan will provide the upgrading plant, the well drilling and the facilities in order for this project to go ahead.
The oil and gas industry is founded on partnerships. Very seldom does any company go it alone. The reason for partnerships is that the capital amounts required are too large. Even Petro-Canada cannot go these things alone. Since billions of dollars are needed, the solution is partnership. Perhaps Petro-Canada has a role to play. It has an interest, and it has capital. As has been said, this company, Husky, is a small one. One of the objectives of Petro-Canada was to assist smaller companies in participating in these things. Here is their chance.
The minister should come forward, take the lead and take the initiative to bring the provinces to the bargaining table. The royalties must be sorted out. Petro-Canada cannot sort out the royalty problems of the provinces any better than Husky can. Petro-Canada is the catalyst to make all this happen. I hope we hear from the minister and the Prime

Minister (Mr. Trudeau) soon. The time is now. The lead time is long and our time is short. We will run out of oil in the 1980's. The absence of leadership and horrendous internal battles accomplish nothing. These battles direct the energies of people toward infighting in Canada, rather than getting on with the job of finding and producing the oil we need.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate tonight. I am glad my chance has come after listening to the oil lobby.
I was somewhat confused today when I heard the contributions of hon. members of the Conservative party. The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) said that there are two Canadian consortiums waiting to develop the Husky project. Where are they? Where have they been? I suspect they are like Moses, hiding in the bulrushes.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said that when the Tories come to power they will disband Petro-Canada. The same thing was said by the hon. member for Calgary Centre. The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Bawden) said that Petro-Canada should be put into the picture. These stories have more positions than the Happy Hooker. I cannot keep up with them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Did you read the book?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
My book was autographed. Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) indicated that past governments have created the problem. He ought to know. He was the minister of mines and resources for Ontario over a long period of time. In his run for the Tory leadership he was defeated, and now he participates at the federal level. We know what he did for the nickel industry. We know the kind of deals he allowed Falconbridge to participate in. That company continued to ship raw materials to Norway for processing. We know the kinds of deals he was into. I am not surprised we are faced with this mess.
The hon. member for Edmonton West blamed Saskatchewan socialists for not being able to develop the resources of that province. Well, the socialists are still in power in Saskatchewan. It was the government of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) which said to the gas companies, "Move over, boys". It was his government which effected the delivery of gas to hundreds of rural communities. His government supplied electricity to hundreds of farms in Saskatchewan, while the private sector was indicating that it could not be done because it was unprofitable. We keep on hearing that same argument.
I was amazed when I saw the Latin inscription on the emblem for Ontario Hydro. The other day when I was at the provincial legislature, I noticed that emblem. It read as follows: "Dona Naturae Pro Populo Sunt". The translation of that is: "To the people belong the resources". I have never heard truer words spoken. Ontario Hydro is an efficient operation. It came into being because of a Tory government.
The hon. member for Edmonton West said that the Petro-Canada intervention into the Husky Oil deal is a government
June 20, 1978

intervention into the private sector. When Peter the Red intervened in the airline business of Alberta and bought the controlling interest of Pacific Western Airlines, no one said that he was a socialist. We all know him as Peter the Red. He recognized a good deal when he saw one. He recognized that the interests of Albertans had to be placed over and above the narrow interest of profit.
The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham indicated that three options were available. One option was that Occidental should take over the company, which he was against. Of course, we are opposed to that idea as well. Then we proposed Petro-Canada ownership of this operation, and he did not agree with that. I am glad the Tories are on the side of the capitalistic oil companies. I am glad they are putting themselves in that spot. The hon. member indicated that there was a third alternative, that is, to get private Canadian entrepreneurs into the operation. Where have they been? Why have they not come forward and made an offer in order to become involved?
That brings me to the gutless wonder who is in the portfolio of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
If it is in the interests of Canadians, as far as Petro-Canada is concerned, for it to become involved in the heavy oil processing operation, why do they not expropriate the company at $45 a share? Somewhere down the road it will become essential for Canadians to have this oil. An investigation ought to be conducted into the mismanagement of Petro-Canada. If it was so essential for Petro-Canada to become involved, why are little handsy-pansy games being played? Why are Canadian taxpayers being taken to the cleaners? The price of a share has now escalated to $52.
There is a principle involved here, and I think it is that principle described in that latin inscription on the coat of arms of Ontario Hydro: Dona Naturae Pro Populo Sunt. That is the crux of the matter. The question is how we view the nonrenewable resources of the country. This involves an important concept. The minister can do all the grinning and smiling he wants. We saw him smile right through the crisis of the Inco and Falconbridge layoffs.
There is a principle involved in respect of non-renewable resources and how we as Canadians view those resources. We on this side of the House happen to recognize that these non-renewable resources represent the key to sources of wealth for future generations of Canadians. In fact, how those resources are used not will determine to a large extent the way in which we are going to conduct our lives in the future.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Our national heritage.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NATURAL RESOURCES-CANADIAN CONTROL OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
There is one thing I have never failed to observe, having lived in the Sudbury basin for some 16 years, and it has followed a regular cycle. The wealth generated by
Natural Resources
those non-renewable resources in Canada is not used for the benefit of Canadians but to extend the wealth of the corporations which have exploited those resources.
It was not surprising, for example, that in 1973 when Inco made some $300 million profit after taxes it used its profit to diversify its operations. Inco bought itself a battery company in the United States, ESB. That is the nature of the capitalist system. That company could not give a damn about laying off 2,000 Canadians in the Sudbury basin. That was not the important matter. The important matter was the extension of the corporation's diversification to increase the size of its empire. That company plans with the interests of Inco and its shareholders in mind.
Let me put the same question to this government. Does it do any planning, and whose interests does it have in mind if it has any plans? This brings us back to the question surrounding non-renewable resources. It seems to me there is only one way to guarantee that the revenues derived from non-renewable resources in this country are put into developing the way of life of Canadians and providing the services for which Canadians have a need, and to which they aspire, and that is through public ownership of those non-renewable resources. There is no question in my mind whatsoever about that, Mr. Speaker.
We have also heard that the private operators, Occidental and Husky, are proposing to put up some money in partnership or in tandem. That is not their main proposal. They are prepared to put up some money and then invite the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta to come into the operation. It seems to me that in the final analysis it is clearly the taxes of the people of Canada which are somehow drained off and used by the private sector for its risk operations.
We all heard the hon. member for Calgary Centre say he has no use at all for public investment. It seems to me I recall that when we were in that great crisis of 1973 and the private sector discovered it could get into the Syncrude operation it came to the federal government for $300 million. Did the federal government obtain any ownership in this regard? The private sector then went to the provinces of Ontario and Alberta and asked them to put up some of the money. It then turned around and said this was too big an operation for little companies and that governments should give financial support.
This is all rather strange because at that time we were being told we had to let the private sector carry out these operations because that sector has the required capital resources. At the same time I find that this government is lending through the Export Development Corporation billions of dollars to multinational corporations in order that they can extend their tentacles into places with such exotic names as Guatemala, The Philippines, Indonesia, Chile and Namibia. Surely there is ample opportunity to invest Canadian taxes in resource development to the benefit of the Canadian public.
We know that the Prime Minister went on record during the 1974 election campaign as promising that we would work toward 50 per cent, preferably 60 per cent, ownership of any new resource development in Canada. That started out as a promise in 1974. We all remember the other promises-for

June 20, 1978
Natural Resources
example, that we would have no wage controls. You remember that, Mr. Speaker, as well as the other promise that he would put public funds into the development of public transportation. He promised Toronto would get $160 million or $200 million. That election is over and it looks like we are into the fifth year of that five-year mandate, and these election promises are now forgotten. Of course, things are different now. The former Conservative member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) has crossed the floor. I think he is a Conservative Trojan stocking horse. 1 think the Tories have planted him on the government side, because we now see all that Tory philosophy emptying out of the belly of this Trojan horse.

Fellows, let us forget about that. This is a hot potato and it is better forgotten. Let the dead bury the dead". He suggests that if they do not talk too much about this the public will not remember the Prime Minister's promise.
We are telling the nation now, because we are on television-

The lights are not off until 10:30, brother. The lights in Nickel Belt are on right now. They haven't put the lights out there yet because we have Ontario Hydro. Thanks to the example set by the CCF government of Saskatchewan, Ontario Hydro decided to electrify the rural areas of Ontario. Maybe we are even doing it with potash.
We know hon. members over there would like to forget about that promise. We are saying right now that the Prime Minister has forgotten that promise, and he has backed away from another promise. He has backed away from the promise to develop, from here on in, all Canadian resources with 50 per cent, preferably 60 per cent, Canadian public participation.

He is still a Tory, the hon. member for Crowfoot, and he sent that memo to his fellow cabinet members, that we should not weep tears for the passing of Petro-Can. I guess he can again shake hands with the hon. member for Edmonton West, the hon. member for Calgary Centre and the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham.
One thing we in this party felt we had obtained during the tenure of the minority government was the promise to establish a Canadian petroleum corporation owned by the Canadian public; a corporation that would get itself involved in the ownership of the petroleum industry from the wellhead to the gas pump. We in this party figure that that was one of the

positive results of the minority government. The other one was getting Thomas Berger appointed as commissioner of the Berger inquiry.
The next thing would be for Canada to get itself involved in the heavy oil development which is going to be needed very much down the road, especially since we can see the cost rising to $25 a barrel. Obviously Husky has sat on these resources and has not had the capital to develop them. Canada now has an opportunity through collective taxes to develop this nonrenewable resource for the benefit of Canadians-not for the benefit of the boys in Texas, not for those privateers that sit to the right, those so-called minions of the corporate oil sector.
1 have had occasion to be in committee with the hon. member for Edmonton West when he huffs and puffs and blows himself into a great big ball to defend the corporate sector.

HEALTH AND WELFARE-EMIGRATION OF DOCTORS FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 8 1 asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), in view of the loss of almost 4,000 doctors from Canada during the years 1967 to 1977 and with increasing losses possible for the future, what plans she had to rectify the situation so that she could assure the Canadian people there will be a sufficient number of doctors graduated to meet, not

June 20, 1978
Adjournment Debate
only the present medical care level, but also the increasing care level of an aging population which requires more geriatricians all the time. Those 60 years of age and older require three times as much health care as they did at 35 years. Added to that is the earlier increase in cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes and other medical problems. Thus more physicians are required.
1 would also like to ask the minister how she expects to keep up the quality of medical care when among those leaving are well-trained professional men, such as teachers and scientists in whom millions of Canadian dollars have been invested in training. Now this knowledge and experience is going south of the border to be an asset there. Many leave with at least two or three decades of earning power before them. That is a prospective $3 million or $5 million, depending on their training. Taking the middle figure of $4 million and taking the minister's figure of 650 doctors emigrating-instead of my own which is much higher-it means that we are giving about $2.6 billion to the United States every year.
Canada simply cannot afford to present those billions of dollars to the United States even though that country is our friend. We do not have the money to enable us to play Santa Claus. Each one of those doctors has cost us between a quarter of a million dollars and half a million dollars, depending upon whether they are trained as general practitioners, have received special training or have gone into scientific research.
There will be a need in Canada for more physicians. According to my information and also that of the minister, there will be no increase in the numbers of doctors graduating even though more will be required. We have now passed the two million mark of those 60 years and over, according to the last figures available in 1976.
The minister has made a statement to the effect that Canada might have too many physicians. That is not correct as the figures include specialist physicians, doctors working in public service, working privately as administrators or for insurance companies, et cetera. Some work part-time. The general practitioner would not average 50 per cent of those, and in actual practice the GP should account for 60 per cent to 70 per cent of physicians. Ruling out part-time physicians, we have one general practitioner for roughly every 2,000 people.
The minister has also stated that the majority of those doctors emigrating were not Canadians. Surely she knows that in January 1977 the United States was asking for and admitting Canadian born doctors and that in the last three years there has been an increase of 300 per cent in those emigrating.
The problem is frightening in that our health care system may break down. It was a Liberal government that brought in the national health program, but over the years it has been using its child like an illegitimate or orphan child. It starves it of research, driving thousands of our young scientists outside the country.
The minister knew the tax position of the doctors. She was well aware that a doctor could not deduct the interest on a

bank loan on this tax return. He could not deduct the cost of mechanical equipment he needed to increase his knowledge, even though it increased his earning power, and as a result of that the government took increased taxes. The minister knew all this because of her previous portfolio as minister of national revenue.
No Canadian born doctor wants to pull up his roots and leave his home and friends. But because of the bureaucracy- the forms that take a quarter of his time to fill in, the wrangling with the bureaucrats of medicine and, finally, the high taxes and frustration, he leaves.
The minister must face those facts. There is a deterioration in the quality of medical service due to the loss of professors and researchers who trained the doctors. There is attrition and the increased service demands of an aging population. There is a breakdown of medical service because of the shortage of doctors, and this is compounded by the increasing number of people over 60 years of age who require service. These days people aged 50 are regarded as being in the geriatric class, and 1 would remind hon. members of this.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has once again brought before this House a matter of continuing importance and concern to all members. The hon. member is considered a specialist in the area of geriatrics and is appreciated for the work he has done in the House and the contribution he has made in this regard.

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-EMIGRATION OF DOCTORS FROM CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-EMIGRATION OF DOCTORS FROM CANADA
speechtext:
The hon. member referred to the emigration of doctors. I am sure he will agree this is a provincial matter and a provincial concern as well. He also referred to the harassment of doctors as a result of the multiplicity of forms they are required to prepare. I am sure he understands from the recent statement by the minister when her estimates were before the committee that this would be reduced to a considerable extent.
With regard to the emigration of doctors, let me say this to the hon. member. If emigration of physicians from Canada during the years 1967 to 1977 is almost 4,000, the loss of manpower in this field has been more than compensated for by immigration which was 10,704. The total number of active civilian physicians in 1968, excluding interns and residents, was 22,969, giving a physician-population ratio of one to 909. In the year 1977 the total figure was 34,860, with a ratio of one to 673.
This ratio of physician supply compares very favourably with most other developed countries, and the attrition arising from emigration and from other reasons has not prevented the steady increase of the ratio. Our medical schools are producing over 1,700 new physicians each year and immigration, which was around 1,000 four years ago, had to be controlled but was still around 300 in 1977. Therefore, there is no indication of shortage of physicians in Canada for the foreseeable future.
June 20, 1978

Concerning the treatment of older people, we see an increased interest amongst the medical profession, nurses and social workers in gerontology. A bureau on aging is being established in the welfare section of the department and a national conference is planned on the subject for the fall. As for geriatrics, a recent survey in March 1977 by the Association of Canadian Medical Colleges shows that medical schools are introducing more and more education of geriatric medicine as an identifiable component of their under-graduate curriculum. The Canadian Association of Gerontology is devoting time and effort, together with other medical associations, to increasing the number of specialists in geriatrics.
On the other hand, the treatment of older people has been carried out in this country for a long time by competent people in every specialty of medicine, except pediatrics and obstetric-gynecology, and by general and family practitioners. It is clear that ophthalmologists and optometrists will continue to treat aging people for their vision problems; that specialists in orthopedic surgery, in urology and in cardiovascular disease and other areas as well will continue to provide good care, together with general and family physicians, in the primary care area; and that a certain number of medicogerontologists and geriatricians will evolve with the increasing demand to look at special problems related to old age. We are certain that the total number of physicians is fully satisfying the demand for candidates in a new specialty which is developing as a support for existing medical care.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-UNFILLED ORDERS FOR OLYMPIC COINS
POST OFFICE-UNFILLED ORDERS FOR OLYMPIC COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) remaining to answer my dissatisfaction with the way the government has handled the Olympic coin program. The Olympic coin program was established by legislation of the federal government. Dealers who purchased and sold Olympic coins were agents of the federal government, and this government is responsible for fulfilling agreements of dealers who received payment and did not supply the coins ordered. What would happen to any corporation in Canada which carried on that kind of business?
The customer relations group, supposedly set up to intercede for purchasers who were cheated out of their coins or could not obtain delivery, admits it cannot now do anything to ensure the orders will be filled. Has the cabinet never heard of bonding companies or of legislation to force dealers to take out a bond? Some of the coin dealers have gone bankrupt. Since the federal government minted and furnished the coins and presumably was paid for them, I maintain that, in addition to being responsible for its agents, the coin dealers, the government should stand behind those who paid for Olympic coins in good faith but were left without coins or compensation.
What action would the government have taken had it not received full payment for the coins purchased by the coin
Adjournment Debate
dealers? Would the government be satisfied to be left without coins or payment?
The Olympic coin report listed a reserve fund of over $18 million for the winding down of the program by the end of this year. The Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) stated he would seek money from the cabinet to refund the purchase price to those who had been cheated. Why place an additional burden on Canadian taxpayers? Is there any reason compensation for the $300,000 worth of unfilled orders cannot be made out of the reserve fund?
A further point arises. Some orders for Olympic coins have been outstanding for over two years. Many purchasers have sent in photostat copies of confirmed orders and their deposited or cashed cheques three or four times, to no avail. Are they not entitled to interest on their money? In some cases the orders amounted to $400 or $500. The government is apparently prepared to set up bureaucracies but is unwilling to stand behind taxpayers who have lost money on a government-initiated program.
Canadians are asking many questions about the whole Olympic coin operation. Many MPs were concerned at the time the relevant legislation was passed. Our cause for concern has now been substantiated. Were any of the unsold Olympic coins eventually sold to a financial institution at face value or at least at a lower rate than the coin dealers or the general public were charged? My information is that a coin dealer offered to purchase unsold coins at a reasonable price, higher than that alleged to have been paid by the financial institution, but did not receive even an acknowledgement of his bid.
There are many questions, so far unanswered, to which I hope the parliamentary secretary will be in a position to reply this evening. 1 am not the only member who has been approached by constituents in an attempt to get this unacceptable transaction sorted out. Although I welcome the minister's assurance that refunds will be made to those who placed orders, 1 cannot agree with the suggestion that additional funds be spent out of the public purse. Surely the balance held in reserve in the Olympic coin fund could be used for that very purpose.
This debate affords the Postmaster General an opportunity to clear the air with regard to what the government intends to do in this scandalous situation. Time is running out. We have only until December 31, 1978, to clear up this intolerable mess.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: POST OFFICE-UNFILLED ORDERS FOR OLYMPIC COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) has made a very strong representation this evening, as he did on June 5, 1978. He will appreciate that when he raised this subject previously the minister indicated, as the hon. member acknowledged in the course of his remarks, that he was very sympathetic toward those who do not seem to have been dealt with fairly. He also pointed out that the Olympic coins corporation has no legal responsibility whatever in respect of these distributors. It is, however, a most unfortunate situation which has developed.

June 20, 1978
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, the Olympic (1976) Act was passed by this House on July 27, 1973. Minting and sale of Olympic coins followed during the next five years. Almost $400 million worth of coins were sold to an estimated two million customers in 63 countries. The result to this point is a profit of $105.5 million which has gone to help cover the cost of the games in Montreal, plus $8.4 million to assist amateur sport.
As hon. members will understand, any sales effort as large as the Olympic coin program, involving several million customers, is very slow to wind down due to illness or death of many of the customers and the complexity of the marketing effort. However, the wind-down program is now at its final stages, and all individual customer complaints have been acted upon, except for approximately 100 cases still to be resolved within the next couple of months. This does not, however, include the special circumstances involving two distributors, Fred Samuels Limited of Montreal and Western Coin Distributors of Regina, Saskatchewan, who experienced financial difficulties and were unable to fill their orders.
The minister has said before that we are sympathetic toward the people who ordered and paid for their coins through these distributors, but the question of finding a way to help them get their coins is complex because of the legalities involved in coins which are legal tender in Canada. Section 5(2) of the Olympic (1976) Act states, and 1 quote:
An Olympic coin shall not be issued or sold by the Government of Canada at less than the face value of the coin and under any arrangement whereby the net consideration received by the Government of Canada for the coin is less than its face value.
As the distributors in question have no money to pay for at least the face value of the coins as referred to in section 5(2), a move by the government to supply coins on an ex gratia basis to the customers might be regarded as violating this section. We do not at this stage have the legal authority to make ex gratia payments to the people whose orders were not filled by the distributors in question.
The officials of the department have been advised to contact Treasury Board to see if anything further can be done to resolve these customers' difficulties.

subtopic: GRAIN-SHORTAGE OF BOXCARS AT CHURCHILL, MAN.
GRAIN-SHORTAGE OF BOXCARS AT CHURCHILL, MAN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to thank the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) for remaining to answer my questions regarding the port of Churchill. He has been a busy man tonight. He is the only one on the benches opposite to answer all our queries.
On June 12 1 asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) what guarantees he could give to ensure the delivery of 30 million bushels of grain from Churchill. I asked that question because of the track record of this government in getting grain to Vancouver, Prince Rupert and other locations, and I thought it was very important to find out if some thought was being given to the port of Churchill. There are less than 100

days in the shipping season at Churchill. The season runs from July 24 to October 20. The minister takes a very partisan approach to anything 1 say about the port of Churchill. If 1 took the approach this government takes to Churchill, we would be lucky if 10 million bushels of grain went through.
The minister said that a record 30 million bushels will reach Churchill this year. I want to put the record straight. That record has never been reached. Last year we came very close to it. We shipped 27.4 million bushels through Churchill, but unfortunately the last two ships which came to the port were diverted to Montreal.
Much work has been done by various groups. Good work is being done by the Hudson Bay Route Association and by the Churchill Development Board in trying to increase grain shipments.
The Hall commission suggests that 55 million bushels of grain could go out through the port of Churchill annually without too much additional expense for the upgrading of that facility. I understand that now the CNR is upgrading two passing tracks between Gillam and Churchill. It will be possible to despatch more trains, and they will not have to have a long waiting time for meeting. What we really need is a firm commitment from this government that when those passing tracks are completed there will be a percentage increase in the amount of grain which goes through the Port of Churchill. Just last week 51 ships were waiting for grain at eastern and western Canadian ports. Twenty-one ocean ships were waiting in Vancouver, ten in Montreal and 20 at St. Lawrence ports. Our ports are experiencing a bottleneck which is worse than that which occurred at the end of World War II. This is costing taxpayers an estimated $2 million a week. Of course, it is mostly the farmers who are paying that. Some ships have been waiting in Vancouver and the St. Lawrence ports for as long as six weeks, and some of them are costing $5,400 a day in demurrage charges.
The cause of the shortage of boxcars to transport grains to these ports has been that many of them are down in the United States, and have been there for some time. Many of the hopper cars are being used for storage of potash instead of for moving grain. The Canadian government is now in the position of not being able to deliver the record 850 million bushels of grain, or $2.5 billion worth, which it sold abroad last year to the Soviet Union, Japan and China. We notice also that another big sale of grain has been made to China. I think the government must understand that we will have to use every port we have in Canada to its full capacity if we want to reach the $1 billion mark in grain shipments out of Canada.
As I have said many times in the House, the port of Churchill is the most efficient grain handling port in Canada. That comment was made by the Board of Grain Commissioners. I cannot for the life of me see why the government could not have made arrangements to extend the season each year. The season was established some 20 years ago when we did not have the technology we now have in the port of Churchill. We
June 20, 1978

now have an ice patrol and every ship is equipped with radar. We could extend the season by one month and thus increase the amount of grain going out of the port by at least 10 per cent per annum over the next five years in order to reach the 50 million bushel mark.
The minister has now decided to have another study carried out with regard to grain movement, called the grain transportation study. I wonder if it is not just a way of slowing things down and taking the pressure off the minister. I would also like to know why we really need this report. 1 would also like to know to whom the terms of reference are extended and who was invited to bid on this study. It is my understanding that some of the people who were invited to bid are in the international world of transportation. Also I notice that the Rod Bryden report on grain handling in the prairies went beyond its terms of reference and included the port of Churchill. Bryden wrote a devastating report against the port of Churchill and its transportation facilities, and it would now appear that he is getting all the creamy jobs from the Department of Transport.
I should like to see the facilities at Churchill used to their maximum capacity and at least 50 million bushels of grain shipped out of there annually.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GRAIN-SHORTAGE OF BOXCARS AT CHURCHILL, MAN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) has once again brought before the House a matter which is of continuing concern, particularly with reference to the openness of the port. There are some 100 days or less when port facilities are open for grain movement purposes. I hope that this year the port will be used to its maximum potential and I am assured that we can expect a third record year.
The hon. member also brought forth a number of other questions which were not contained in his original question. I hope these questions can be answered at a later date.
I would like to assure the House that every effort will be made to again use the port of Churchill to the maximum extent for the third year in a row. There is currently pressure on all parts of the transportation system to move the grain that has been sold this crop year. However, Churchill will most likely find itself again in the advantageous position of experiencing its greatest demand on the transportation system
Adjournment Debate
late in the crop year after the tight situation elsewhere has eased. The Churchill season from July to October normally requires boxcars after the system has had time to recover from the delays which often occur during the winter. This situation can be expected to occur again this year.
The government is committed to maximizing the use of the port of Churchill. In our current rehabilitation program for prairie rail lines, $1,610,000 has been allotted by the federal government to improve the rail line into Churchill. The work to be undertaken involves bank widening and drainage, rail relay and extending the sidings along the line. These improvements are expected to double the capacity of the port.
The grain transportation situation is under constant review by the government. Continually we are searching for ways to improve efficiency in the utilization of present facilities. Examples of the benefits of this study abound. The most obvious example of the improvements which have been made is the fact that car turnaround time for grains moving to export position has been reduced to 17 or 18 days from the 22.9 days determined by the Hall commission report one year ago. The government will continue to analyse the system looking for new ways of improving its operation, with a view to providing adequate facilities to moving to market the increasing production which is expected in the next few years.
Recently the government has announced an intensive investigation of the operating procedures used by the railroads, grain handling companies and the Canadian Wheat Board, as they work together moving Canada's grain production to market. This project is expected to provide additional recommendations which will further improve the utilization of the railroad facilities currently available.
Through its purchase of 8,000 hopper cars and its commitment to a $700 million rehabilitation program, the government has shown a willingness to step in and provide the necessary transportation facilities when warranted.
